title: Falcons trade for Bears defensive lineman Gervon Dexter
summary: Well, can’t say I expected that one. The Atlanta Falcons have traded Clark Phillips and a 2027 fifth round pick to the Chicago Bears for defensive tackle Gervon Dexter, adding more beef and pressure to their defensive front for a day three pick and a cornerback who was not guaranteed to make the roster. Adam […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - JANUARY 10: Gervon Dexter Sr. #99 of the Chicago Bears runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, can’t say I expected that one. The Atlanta Falcons have traded Clark Phillips and a 2027 fifth round pick to the Chicago Bears for defensive tackle Gervon Dexter, adding more beef and pressure to their defensive front for a day three pick and a cornerback who was not guaranteed to make the roster. Adam Schefter inevitably had the deal and its terms first. Trade terms, per source: 🏈Bears receive CB Clark Phillips III and a fifth-round pick. 🏈Falcons receive DT Gervon Dexter. https://t.co/NG23VcLOjg — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) August 30, 2026 Dexter was a player I liked quite a bit in the 2023 NFL Draft, but he landed in Chicago in the second round. Listed at 6’6” and 326 pounds, Dexter has played in 49 of a possible 51 games since landing in the league and has 13.5 sacks, including six a year ago, and offers a proven ability to get after the quarterback from the interior. Defensive line coach Nate Ollie, who got this Falcons defense sacking quarterbacks at a franchise record clip in 2025, now gets another piece to help the Falcons keep the pace. It’s an especially big deal with Jalon Walker out for the season and James Pearce Jr. suspended for about half the season, but it also sets the Falcons up for an absolutely fearsome interior pass rush in 2026 with Brandon Dorlus, LaCale London, Maason Smith, and Chris Williams also in the rotation. Da’Shawn Hand, who figures to be a major piece of the rotation, is working his way back from an injury. Why were the Bears ready to let Dexter go? One suspects that Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham, who would have been involved in drafting Dexter, may have been more fond of him than the current staff and Bears GM Ryan Poles. Dexter’s faced consistent criticism for inconsistent tackling and performance against the run, something the Falcons will hope to see improvement from him on, but on paper it does not make sense for a Bears defense that isn’t exactly stacked up front to part with a still-young player who generates pressure regardless. One suspects the Bears weren’t planning to give him a new deal and felt he wasn’t the sort of high-level defensive lineman they needed to build around, but it’s still a surprising decision given their own issues and the lack of high-level compensation. They appear to like their former Falcons defensive tackles, as they have Grady Jarrett and just signed Kentavius Street this offseason. The Falcons have their first-through-fourth round picks but have been surprisingly cavalier about trading Day 3 selections this offseason, having moved a sixth round pick for Wanya Morris and now a fifth for Dexter. They do have a seventh rounder originally from the Jets in that Morris deal, as the previous front office traded a 2027 7th for Mike Jerrell in 2025. Phillips might benefit from a change of scenery, but the former fourth round pick had never delivered on his early promise in Atlanta and was in danger of being outright cut this summer after a mixed preseason; I certainly wish him well in Chicago. Dexter’s contract will expire after this season, setting up a decision for the Falcons. I suspect they’ll gladly bring him back if he’s as good or better than he was in 2025 in Chicago, though they’ll hope to see better from him against the run before committing big dollars. Regardless, the Falcons just paid a very fair price for a very good player who should help the defense in 2026, and that kind of addition was sorely needed given the attrition to this team’s pass rush. Give Dexter a warm welcome, and let’s hope he’s great here.

full_text: RALEIGH, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 21: CJ Bailey #11 of the NC State Wolfpack looks to pass the ball during the first half of a football game against the Florida State Seminoles at Carter-Finley Stadium on November 21, 2025 in Raleigh, North Carolina. But the college scouts are already getting ready to head all over the world for Week 0 action, including Dublin, Ireland, and the start of year two of Bill Belichick and the North Carolina Tar Heels. Gets the OL’s outside shoulder tip & snatch/swims Deal reducing his pad surface, pressures QB & meets Namdi Obiazor in the backfield for the sack! #PassRush #GoFrogs #BleedPurple @_CoachJmac pic.twitter.com/i1CRcgLsO2 — DLineVids (@dlinevids1) August 31, 2024 While Maason Smith has had a solid training camp, there isn’t much along the defensive line for the Falcons, outside of LaCale London. Both Da’Shawn Hand and Chris Williams have shown flashes of being solid pieces, and they may have something in UDFA Carlos Allen, Jr., but there are certainly spots that can be upgraded for the future. Markis Deal is a powerful run defender who towers at 6’5”, 325 pounds. If he can show a bit more pass-rush juice this season, starting against the Tar Heels, he may be able to play himself into early day-three status or even crack some top-100s as a potential two- to three-down lineman. San Jose State @ USC – Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, Los Angeles, CA – 3 pm EST – NBC Jayden Maiava, QB, USC Jayden Maiava (6’4 220) USC ✅ Toughness in the pocket ✅ Keeps his eyes down the field when moving out of the pocket ✅ 72.3% adjusted completion rate during the 2025 season ✅ Knows how and when to vary the velocity of his throws ✅ Over 3,700 passing yards and 24 passing… pic.twitter.com/N9SnMgdJ8z — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) May 25, 2026 Until we get this quarterback situation dealt with, there will be a lot of giving virtually any quarterback to the Falcons. However, even if the Falcons do figure it out with either Penix or Tua, Maiava may be a solid addition to the quarterback room if we, for some ungodly reason, don’t keep UDFA Jack Strand as QB3 and allow him to get sniped on the waiver wire. Maiava is an experienced college quarterback who can put good touch on the football, leading to a variety of throws in his arsenal, especially outside the pocket. If he shows that he can keep the ball out of harm’s way, not only will he boost his draft stock, but the sky is the limit on where this Lincoln Riley-led USC team can go. title: Falcons – Dolphins recap: To the regular season we go
summary: As a football game, it was pretty artless, with some nice stretches from the defense and a handful of big plays on offense and special teams adding a little excitement to a contest that was otherwise plodding, penalty-ridden, and low-scoring. As an audition for this Falcons roster, it told many tales, some of them tragic […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - AUGUST 28: Tua Tagovailoa #1 of the Atlanta Falcons throws against the Miami Dolphins during the first half at Hard Rock Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images As a football game, it was pretty artless, with some nice stretches from the defense and a handful of big plays on offense and special teams adding a little excitement to a contest that was otherwise plodding, penalty-ridden, and low-scoring. As an audition for this Falcons roster, it told many tales, some of them tragic and some of them terrific. That was the third preseason game in a nutshell, with the Falcons dispatching the hapless Dolphins 17-12. Atlanta’s starters went out there against Miami’s backups and struck first, with Brian Robinson capping off a Tua Tagovailoa-led drive with a score. Tua would then fumble an iffy snap from Corey Levin to derail a drive, marring an otherwise effective but unexciting night featuring a lot of short passes, and then the backups were in. Cooper Rush mostly stuck to short passes himself, with a nice quick toss to Jack Velling for a touchdown, but uncorked a beautiful in-stride ball to Tyler Goodson that set up a field goal before the half. The 17 points were all the Falcons would score, as the second half featured an extremely bland gameplan for Jack Strand—though he was still fairly sharp, minus an interception that went off Nate Carter’s hands and into the air for Miami—and some poor defense that set up a pair of Dolphins field goal drives. There are no big takeaways for the starters, except for the fact that it was nice to see them largely dominate Miami’s reserves and the stern warning Tua must receive over the number of fumbled snaps he’s had this summer. The reserves are a different story, given that players like Goodson, Velling, Harold Perkins Jr., Chris Williams, and Rush did well enough to make a big push for roster spots, while others scuffled mightily. If the coaching staff was wavering on who to keep around at positions like cornerback and running back, tonight probably provided them with the data points they needed to make a decision. And blessedly, preseason is now over. Roster cuts are tough because good players and good people ultimately will get the axe, but knowing the shape of the roster lets us properly evaluate what the team will be capable of. Knowing the practice squad helps us get a better sense of who the Falcons want to develop and what break-in-case-of-emergency options exist for them. All of that is welcome, especially for a first year front office and staff, even if I’ll undoubtedly be sad to see many Falcons who spent the spring and summer here headed elsewhere. While we wait for news of cuts and additions both before and after the Sunday cutdown deadline, let’s dive in to the full recap. The next time we gather to talk about a game, it will be one that counts in the NFC South standings. The Good The Falcons almost seemed like they were keeping Jack Strand corked in this one, so the heavy lifting fell to Cooper Rush. While Rush was also seemingly held in check by a vanilla game plan early on and missed a couple of short throws, he led the offense to two scoring drives and had two of the best throws of the night for any quarterback on a sharp slant to Jack Velling for a touchdown and a beautiful ball to Tyler Goodson for the long gain before the half that set up a field goal. I don’t know Atlanta’s plans at quarterback, but at this point, Rush hasn’t done anything to play himself out of a QB3 role. It’s just a question of whether the Falcons view Strand’s upside as significant enough to part ways with Rush or try to sneak him on to the practice squad. For what it’s worth, I think they very well might. Tyler Goodson rocks. Once again he looked terrific in this one, with the highlight play coming in the second quarter on a pretty ball from Cooper Rush that hit him in stride downfield, with Goodson hitting an insane spin move to pick up more yards and then smartly spiking it to set up a field goal try right before the half. He’s the third running back and has been good enough that he might get a little regular season work even with the Robinsons healthy. Vinny Anthony and Chris Blair are my picks for WR5/6, if the Falcons keep that many guys. Blair continues to run effective routes and look very sure-handed, while Anthony has been dynamic as a receiver and damn good as a returner, with the patience and vision to turn good blocking into a late kick return that went past midfield. Both guys deserve spots, but if there’s only one up for grabs, Anthony’s return value might give him the edge. If Tua is the quarterback, it looks likely Jahan Dotson will get plenty of run. He was a favored security blanket during Tua’s short starting stint in this one, and looked good and decisive in that role. Kyle Pitts looked really good in this one. He got loose on a screen for a big pickup early on and easily led the team in receiving yardage, showcasing those long strides that let him simply outrun defenders and the sure hands that give him an opportunity in the first place. In an offense built to showcase tight ends and looking healthy and sure of himself, Pitts could be headed for a monster season. Nick Muse is a solid blocking tight end and player overall, and I think the Falcons will try to keep him around in some capacity. But it was Jack Velling who did a lot of damage in this one as a receiver, and a really solid summer has given the rookie undrafted free agent a genuine shot to stick around as the fourth tight end. The only question is whether the Falcons will keep four on the 53 man roster—unlikely, in my opinion—or sneak him on to the practice squad. I loved Harold Perkins Jr. pursuing Cam Miller to the ends of the earth on a third down in the second quarter. This is the third preseason game and the stakes seem low, but Perkins treated every Miller juke as a personal affront and eventually got him, sacking him and forcing a fumble that fell out of bounds. That relentlessness is going to stand out for this coaching staff, and Perkins did open as a starter in this one. Chris Williams has been heating up as the summer has gone along. He’s shown some legitimate pass rushing ability, getting after Cam Miller repeatedly in this one, and then blocking a field goal try early on in the game. He’s making this roster and should be a fun player in a go get ‘em front. Cameron Thomas has been another good addition, making the most of his early down snaps and picking up a pretty effortless sack tonight. If he can get home consistently and deliver that solid work against the run, the Falcons have another very useful piece. Quietly, the Falcons run defense has looked pretty good this summer, with a few tough stretches against the Broncos looking like the only knock against this front. I don’t know if that will translate to the regular season just yet, but it’s an encouraging sign. Josh Woods should make the roster. I know Channing Tindall has ties to special teams coordinator Craig Aukerman, but Woods is a very capable special teamer and has played his ass off on defense all preseason long. The highlight in this one was a hustle play where he came in to recover a high snap and fumble by quarterback Mark Gronowski, another testament to his instincts and effort. With zero offense intended to Tindall or JD Bertrand, Woods has been doing this long enough and well enough that I’d hope he would make it ahead of either of them. James Pearce Jr. got two sacks working against the deep reserves, but we know he can also do that against the starters. The Falcons are going to miss him through the first half of the season, but the hope is that all goes well during his suspension, he abides by the term of his trial diversion program, and we see him later in the year. The Falcons have some good problems at safety, where Sydney Brown and Natrone Brooks offer positional…

title: Building the perfect 53-man roster for the 2026 Baltimore Ravens
summary: With roster cuts approaching, this isn’t necessarily a prediction of exactly what the Ravens will do. It’s how I would construct Baltimore’s initial 53-man roster based on preseason performance, positional value, roster flexibility, and the likelihood of certain players making it through waivers. The 53 Offense — 24 QB: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley RB: Derrick […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Ethan Burke #45 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on before the preseason game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images With roster cuts approaching, this isn’t necessarily a prediction of exactly what the Ravens will do. It’s how I would construct Baltimore’s initial 53-man roster based on preseason performance, positional value, roster flexibility, and the likelihood of certain players making it through waivers. The 53 Offense — 24 QB: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley RB: Derrick Henry, Justice Hill, Adam Randall WR: Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, Ja’Kobi Lane, Devontez Walker, LaJohntay Wester, Elijah Sarratt TE: Mark Andrews, Josh Cuevas, Matthew Hibner, Durham Smythe OL: Ronnie Stanley, Roger Rosengarten, Vega Ioane, John Simpson, Jovaughn Gwyn, Ethan Pocic, Carson Vinson, Diego Pounds, Emery Jones Jr. Defense — 26 DL: Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, Aeneas Peebles, Rayshaun Benny, Broderick Washington LB: Roquan Smith, Trenton Simpson, Jay Higgins, Teddye Buchanan OLB: Trey Hendrickson, Zion Young, Mike Green, Tavius Robinson, Ethan Burke, Kaimon Rucker CB: Nate Wiggins, Marlon Humphrey, Chidobe Awuzie, T.J. Tampa, Chandler Rivers, Keyon Martin, Bilhal Kone S: Kyle Hamilton, Malaki Starks, Jaylin Hawkins, Keondre Jackson Specialists K: Tyler Loop P: Ryan Eckley LS: Nick Moore Key Decisions Joe Fagnano, QB3 Joe Fagnano has done just about everything he could have this preseason to make the Ravens seriously consider carrying a third quarterback. He currently ranks third in the NFL in preseason passing yards and fifth in passer rating, putting together the type of performance you want to see from a developmental quarterback fighting for a roster spot. The question isn’t whether Fagnano has played well enough. It’s whether keeping a developmental QB who may never see the field this season provides more value than using that roster spot on a defensive lineman or outside linebacker who could contribute immediately. For me, it doesn’t. The chances of Fagnano being poached are relatively low, and if Baltimore can get him back onto the practice squad, he can continue developing within the system while providing an emergency third-quarterback option on game day. His preseason has earned him consideration, but with the numbers getting tight elsewhere, I would use the roster spot at a premium position. How to handle Nnamdi Madubuike The first question here is obvious: where is Nnamdi Madubuike? To this point, we’ve seen positive trends toward Madubuike getting healthy and eventually returning to the lineup. But there is very little reason to rush that process simply to get him onto the field in Week 1. If bringing him back immediately means increasing the possibility of reinjury or having to significantly limit his workload just to keep him healthy, Baltimore would be better served taking the patient approach. I would place Madubuike on short-term IR and allow him to continue working toward being fully healthy rather than merely healthy enough to play. That also gives Baltimore some flexibility along the defensive line. The Ravens could potentially work out a handshake agreement with John Jenkins, bring him back through the practice squad and maintain experienced interior depth while waiting for Madubuike’s return. The goal shouldn’t be getting Madubuike back as quickly as possible. It should be getting him back in a position where he can remain on the field. Why keep six outside linebackers? I have Baltimore carrying six edge rushers, which may initially look excessive. There’s a reason for it. Ethan Burke has shown legitimate, competent edge-rusher ability throughout the preseason while possessing the versatility traditionally valued in a Ravens outside linebacker. He can rush from the edge, reduce inside, operate from a two-point stance and drop into coverage. At his size, he also brings additional value on special teams. That versatility makes him difficult for me to cut. Kaimon Rucker presents a different argument. Rucker has flashed legitimate designated-pass-rusher upside this preseason and gives Baltimore another developmental speed-rush option. The Ravens don’t have a true backup for Mike Green’s role on the roster. With edge rusher being a premium position around the league, exposing a young pass rusher who has already flashed developmental upside to waivers is an unnecessary gamble. Baltimore can find replacement-level depth at several positions after cuts. Finding young players who can rush the passer is much more difficult. That’s ultimately why both Burke and Rucker make my 53. Baltimore enters the season with Hendrickson, Young, Green and Robinson as its primary rotation while Burke provides positional and special-teams versatility and Rucker develops as a designated pass-rush option. For a defense that wants to consistently create pressure without being dependent on the blitz, I’d rather have one too many edge rushers than one too few.

And this year, cutdown day looks a little different. NFL teams must reduce their rosters to 53 players by 6 p.m. EDT on Sunday, August 30, in a change from the Tuesday deadline we’ve grown accustomed to in recent years. That means plenty of players we’ve watched throughout training camp and the preseason are about to be released. But before Bills Mafia starts saying goodbye, remember: Cut doesn’t necessarily mean gone. For some players, Sunday will simply be the first step toward returning to Buffalo on the practice squad. Buffalo can’t simply trim its roster to 53 and quietly move everyone else it likes onto the practice squad. For many players, there’s an important stop in between: Waivers. Players with fewer than four accrued NFL seasons must pass through waivers after they’re released. That gives the other 31 teams an opportunity to claim them. If a player is claimed, he must join that team’s 53-man roster. If nobody claims him, he clears waivers and becomes free to sign with ANY practice squad. Veterans with four or more accrued seasons don’t go through that same process at final cuts. Once released, they’re free to negotiate with another team immediately, or stay on with the Bills practice squad. Waiver claims following this year’s final roster cuts are due by 1 p.m. EDT on Monday, August 31. Once those claims are processed, teams can begin assembling their practice squads. Building Buffalo’s practice squad Once the waiver process is complete, the Bills can begin filling their practice squad. Teams can carry 16 practice-squad players, and Buffalo can potentially have a 17th spot for an eligible International Player. That extra designation matters for my projection because Travis Clayton remains part of the International Player Pathway (IPP) program. Despite what the name might suggest, the practice squad isn’t reserved entirely for rookies and developmental projects. NFL rules allow teams to carry up to six players with unlimited accrued seasons, giving Buffalo the flexibility to mix younger developmental players with experienced veterans. That’s an important distinction. A practice squad should contain players the Bills hope to develop for the future, but it also needs players who can help them right now. Because once the regular season begins, that practice squad becomes part developmental program, and part emergency supply. When the Bills need reinforcements This is where the modern practice squad becomes especially valuable. The Bills can elevate two practice-squad players for a game each week without permanently signing them to the 53-man roster. After the game, those players revert back to the practice squad without having to clear waivers. An individual player can receive that standard elevation up to three times during the regular season. If the team wants him available for a fourth game, they have to sign him to the active roster. It’s not necessarily about identifying the 16 best players who didn’t make the 53. Buffalo needs players who can step into different roles when injuries inevitably happen. That means positional depth matters. Special teams matter. Familiarity with the system matters. Versatility matters. And there’s another wrinkle to all of this: The team isn’t guaranteed to keep those players all season. Yes, another team can take them. Practice-squad players aren’t permanently protected from the rest of the NFL. Another team can sign a player from a practice squad, but there’s an important catch: that team has to sign him to its active roster. It can’t simply move him from Buffalo’s practice squad onto its own. And that brings us to the players I think Buffalo will try to keep. Looking at my final 53-man roster projection, these are the players I believe Buffalo could try to bring back: QB: Shane Buechele RB: Ian Wheeler WR: Trent Sherfield, Ja’Mori Maclin, Dante Pettis, Stephen Gosnell (if room) TE: Keleki Latu OL: Ar’maj Reed-Adams, Sedrick Van Pran-Granger (if not IR), Nick Broeker DL: Greg Gaines, Travis Clayton (IPP) EDGE: Mike Danna (if not traded) , Andre Jones Jr. LB: Joe Andreessen (if not on 53) CB: Te’Cory Couch, Toriano Pride Jr. Predicting a practice squad before roster cuts is very different from predicting the 53-man roster because a team doesn’t completely control the outcome. Some of these players first have to make it through waivers. Another team could claim one. A veteran could choose another opportunity. Buffalo could also claim someone released elsewhere. And there could still be a trade or two that changes the equation. Who could be tougher to keep? The wide receivers immediately jump out. I have Sherfield, Maclin and Pettis projected to the practice squad, with Gosnell included if Buffalo can find room. That’s a lot of receivers to keep, especially when the Bills will need enough positional balance on the practice squad to cover injuries elsewhere. As a vested veteran, Sherfield does not need to clear waivers. The Bills could elevate him for three weeks while evaluating other positions. Then there’s Mike Danna, whose situation may never reach the practice squad. With Buffalo’s crowded edge group, Danna has been mentioned as a potential trade or release candidate heading into final cuts. If Beane can find a trade partner, getting something in return makes more sense than simply releasing him and hoping he’s available afterward. Joe Andreessen is almost the opposite situation. He already knows Buffalo’s defense, offers linebacker depth and can contribute on special teams. That’s exactly the type of player who makes sense to keep close because his value isn’t limited to one role. There’s a good chance Andreessen is on the 53. And then there’s Travis Clayton. Because of his IPP designation, keeping him doesn’t necessarily force Buffalo to choose between him and one of the other players on this list. That 17th spot gives the Bills another developmental opportunity without sacrificing one of the traditional 16. Don’t forget about everyone else’s cuts There’s one final piece of the practice-squad puzzle that’s easy to overlook. Buffalo isn’t only evaluating its own players this weekend. While we’re debating which Bills deserve to come back, Beane and his staff will be watching hundreds of players released by the NFL’s other 31 teams. Someone Buffalo liked coming out of college could become available. A team could unexpectedly release a veteran at a position where the Bills need depth. Another player might simply fit Buffalo’s roster better than someone the Bills just spent the entire summer developing. That’s why the first practice squad isn’t necessarily going to be made up entirely of Bills training-camp cuts. The practice squad isn’t really football’s waiting room anymore. It’s an extension of the roster.
author: Sara Larson

title: PUP, IR, NFI and even a suspension could give Buffalo Bills some additional roster flexibility Sunday
summary: The preseason is over, which means we have reached one of my favorite parts of roster construction: trying to figure out what Brandon Beane is doing before Brandon Beane tells us what Brandon Beane is doing. By Sunday, August 30 at 6 p.m. ET, the Buffalo Bills must reduce their roster to 53 players.Except getting […]
full_text: The preseason is over, which means we have reached one of my favorite parts of roster construction: trying to figure out what Brandon Beane is doing before Brandon Beane tells us what Brandon Beane is doing. By Sunday, August 30 at 6 p.m. ET, the Buffalo Bills must reduce their roster to 53 players.Except getting to 53 isn’t quite as simple as counting to 53. Injuries complicate everything. So do suspensions. That’s where terms like PUP, Reserve/PUP, IR, NFI, designated to return and the Reserve/Suspended list start flying around Bills Mafia. The rules aren’t terribly difficult once they’re separated, but the NFL has changed them several times, including an important PUP change for 2026. So here’s what you need to know. The Physically Unable to Perform list (PUP) The easiest way to remember PUP: A player must enter training camp on PUP to remain eligible for PUP. PUP is for players who report to camp with a football-related injury and aren’t medically cleared to practice. During training camp they’re placed on Active/PUP, where they count against the offseason roster limit and can be activated at any time. But once a player practices, that door closes. He can’t be placed back on PUP later. If he’s still unable to play when Buffalo establishes its 53-man roster, he can be transferred to Reserve/PUP, where he doesn’t count against the 53 but must miss at least the first four games. New in 2026: Practice after Game 2. Play after Game 4. A player on Reserve/PUP can now begin his 21-day practice window after his team’s second regular-season game. He still cannot play until four games have elapsed. But remember, once the practice window opens, the player has only those 21 days to be moved from reserve to active or their season is over, so timing is paramount. For Buffalo, Tyrell Shavers is the player to watch. Shavers has remained on PUP throughout the summer after an ACL injury in January, keeping him eligible for Reserve/PUP at roster cutdowns. Under the new rule, Buffalo could theoretically open his practice window after Week 2… but it’s highly doubtful. The important part is that Buffalo now has the option. The Bills aren’t required to open that window as soon as Shavers becomes eligible. They will take their time. What about NFI? You’ll sometimes see NFI , or the Non-Football Injury/Illness list, grouped with PUP. The easiest distinction is the cause: Football-related injury; PUP. Injury or illness that didn’t result from NFL football activities?; NFI. Like PUP, players must be placed on the appropriate list before participating in training camp practice to remain eligible for the reserve version. For fans, just think of NFI as PUP’s non-football cousin. Injured Reserve is where things get interesting Unlike PUP, a player doesn’t have to enter training camp injured to land on IR. He can practice all summer, play in the preseason, get injured and then require IR. The important question becomes when Buffalo places him there. Normally, placing a player on IR before the initial 53 is established ends his season. But there’s an important exception: Teams can designate up to two players to return while making its final roster reduction. Those players can go directly to IR without first taking up spots on the initial 53 and remain eligible to return. That saves Buffalo from the old roster shuffle of keeping an injured player on the initial 53, cutting someone the Bills actually wanted, moving the injured player to IR and then hoping the other player was still available to re-sign. There is a catch though: Those two designations count against Buffalo’s season-long allotment of eight return designations. They aren’t freebies. The Bills may have three candidates for those two IR spots This is where Sunday’s roster decisions become particularly interesting. Buffalo can use two pre-cutdown IR designations, and there appear to be three legitimate candidates. OT Jude Bowry The rookie fourth-round pick suffered a foot/leg injury during the preseason and has since been seen in a walking boot. Bowry is exactly the type of player this rule can help protect. C Sedrick Van Pran-Granger Van Pran-Granger has also missed valuable practice time leading into roster cuts. If Buffalo believes he needs several more weeks before he’s ready, he becomes another logical candidate for one of the two spots. RB Ty Johnson Then there’s Johnson, who has been sidelined with a knee injury. If the Bills don’t believe he’ll be ready early in the season, he gives Brandon Beane a third player to consider. Remember, IR guarantees Johnson would miss at least four games. If Buffalo believes he could return sooner than that, carrying him on the active roster may make more sense. And then there’s Phidarian Mathis Because apparently PUP, NFI and IR aren’t enough acronyms and roster exceptions for one article. Let’s add SSPD. Bills defensive tackle Phidarian Mathis has been suspended for the first three games of the 2026 season for violating the NFL’s Substances of Abuse Policy. Here’s the important roster part: Once Mathis is placed on Reserve/Suspended, he doesn’t count against Buffalo’s 53-man roster during his suspension. That gives the Bills another temporary roster spot. When Mathis is reinstated, the Bills will need to create room for him on the active roster IF they want to activate him. But for the first three games, his suspension creates some temporary flexibility. In other words, Brandon Beane could potentially use that spot to keep another defensive lineman, young prospect or player he doesn’t want to expose to waivers. In-season IR rules During the regular season, teams have eight return designations available from applicable reserve lists. That number can increase to 10 in the postseason. A player can be designated for return twice, but each return counts separately toward the team’s total. And a reminder: Buffalo’s two pre-cutdown designations count against the eight. For a return-eligible player placed on IR, the minimum absence is four games. Not four weeks. Four games. Bye weeks don’t count. And once Buffalo opens an IR player’s practice window, the Bills have 21 days to activate him to the 53-man roster. Why all of this matters Sunday This is where CBA rules become roster strategy. Buffalo potentially has Shavers headed to Reserve/PUP, Mathis headed to Reserve/Suspended and three players who could be considered for the two IR return designations. None of those players would occupy spots on Buffalo’s active 53 while on those respective reserve lists. That can create room for players who otherwise might not survive Sunday’s cuts. Maybe it’s an extra defensive lineman. Maybe it’s a sixth wide receiver. Maybe it’s a young defensive back Buffalo doesn’t want to expose to waivers. That’s why the Bills aren’t simply identifying their 53 best players. They’re figuring out how to retain as many players as possible while navigating injuries, suspensions and the CBA rules available to them. The initial 53 is exactly that: initial. Knowing Brandon Beane, it might remain intact just long enough for us to write about it or make a graphic before he changes it. PUP, IR and the bottom line When Buffalo starts announcing transactions Sunday, don’t just look at who was “cut.” Pay attention to where everyone goes. Shavers should head to Reserve/PUP. Mathis will begin serving his three-game suspension. And Buffalo could have a fascinating decision involving Bowry, Van Pran-Granger and Johnson for two available pre-cutdown IR return designations. Those moves could open several roster spots without the Bills actually losing those players. That’s what makes cutdown day more than simply counting backward from 90 to 53. It’s roster chess. And Brandon Beane has a few pieces he can temporarily move off the board before deciding exactly what his opening 53 will look like.
author: Sara Larson

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: tackle Dion Dawkins
summary: The Buffalo Bills have been remarkably stable along the offensive line over the last few seasons. Between right guard O’Cyrus Torrence, who has taken nearly every snap on offense throughout his career, center Connor McGovern, who has played through myriad injuries and still been remarkably effective, and right tackle Spencer Brown, who overcame an early-career […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: Dion Dawkins #73 of the Buffalo Bills signs autographs for fans on the way to the field during training camp at St. John Fisher University on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have been remarkably stable along the offensive line over the last few seasons. Between right guard O’Cyrus Torrence, who has taken nearly every snap on offense throughout his career, center Connor McGovern, who has played through myriad injuries and still been remarkably effective, and right tackle Spencer Brown, who overcame an early-career bout with the injury bug to settle in as an elite protector, the Bills have multiple incredible linemen up front. That’s obviously missing one very important, very consistent, and very good player. The left tackle is not only the most tenured player on Buffalo’s offense, but he trails only Reid Ferguson as the player who has been on the team for the longest amount of time. Now entering his tenth season, the man tasked with protecting quarterback Josh Allen’s blind side is playing at a lower weight, something he hopes will maximize his enormous talent. You already Schnow who the subject of today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days” is. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Dion Dawkins Number: 73 Position: T Height/Weight: 6’5” 320 lbs. Age: 32 (33 on 4/26/2027) Experience/Draft: 10; selected by Buffalo in the second round (No. 63 overall) of the 2017 NFL Draft College: Temple Acquired: Second-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Dawkins enters the second year of a three-year, $60.06 million extension that he signed in March of 2024. For the 2026 season, his cap hit is $24,837,833. That cap number trails only Josh Allen on Buffalo’s roster. If the Bills were to release Dawkins, they would carry a dead cap hit of $22,446,833 this year. 2025 Recap: Dawkins once again entered the year as Buffalo’s starting left tackle, and he made his fifth straight Pro Bowl after another strong season. Dawkins suffered a concussion during Buffalo’s 23-19 loss at the Houston Texans, and while he was cleared to return to the game, he dealt with symptoms the following day. Those symptoms caused him to miss Buffalo’s game at the Pittsburgh Steelers the following week. Dawkins was cleared to return the week after against the Cleveland Browns, though, and he only sat out one more game: Buffalo’s regular-season finale where they rested multiple starters. Continuing a troubling trend, Dawkins was flagged for double-digit penalties for the second straight season. False starts have been an issue, as he’s been called for 16 of them over the last two years alone. For context, he had been called for 14 false starts in his first seven seasons combined. Pro Football Focus ranked him as the No. 26 tackle overall out of 89 qualifiers, grading him at a 74.1 for the season. He was ranked much higher in pass blocking (81.8; No. 7 overall) than he did run blocking (66; No. 44 overall). Positional outlook: Dawkins is one of five players listed at tackle. Spencer Brown and Chase Lundt are listed exclusively at tackle, like Dawkins is, while Jude Bowry and Tylan Grable are listed at tackle/guard. 2026 Offseason: Dawkins is healthy and he has participated in training camp practices. He said he is down around 45 pounds from last season, and while his listed weight was 320 lbs. as it’s always been, I don’t think he currently weighs 275 lbs. That tells me that he was playing above his listed weight last season, and frankly, that tracks given how he looked physically last season. 2026 Season outlook: Entering his tenth season, it’s a positive sign that Dawkins has taken steps to improve his overall health, quickness, and agility this offseason. Training camp is loaded with players who say they are in the best shape of their lives, but Dawkins does look better than he did last year. He said that he wanted to be lighter and more agile than he was last year, and that commitment to his pjhysical conditioning should go a long way towards helping him be the best version of himself this year. Dawkins is a vital part of what the Bills do. He’s a vocal leader on and off the field, and he’s one of their most consistent players on Sundays. He is going to start every game when he’s healthy, and he has done a good job remaining available throughout his career. The 2026 season holds very few questions as to Dawkins’ role. However, given his age and the realities of the business of football, it’s fair to wonder whether the 2026 season will be his last in Buffalo. The Bills could choose to hand the left tackle spot to someone like Bowry, who has impressed in camp, and save nearly $12 million on the salary cap by moving on from Dawkins next season. Now, if Dion is still playing at a high level, this isn’t something I think I would do. His importance to the team reaches far beyond the playing field. However, Buffalo is going to be tight to the cap again next year, and they have committed big resources to three younger offensive linemen in Spencer Brown, O’Cyrus Torrence, and Connor McGovern. The Bills could have redone Dawkins’ contract this offseason, but rather than lower his 2026 cap hit and kick salary down the road, they chose to keep his number high this year. That could indicate that they don’t know what they want to do with Dawkins moving forward. This whole line of thinking could also be much ado about nothing. Whatever the future holds, the present iteration of the Buffalo Bills needs No. 73 to be the best version of himself. Dawkins seems to be up to the challenge.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 14 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 10: Mike Minter #30 of the Carolina Panthers stands on the field during the game against the New York Giants on December 10, 2006, at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo By Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #14. Mike Minter A lot of times it feels like Carolina Panthers fans long for the days of Mike Minter at safety. It’s a position the organization has historically placed little value in. Minter is the peak of that position in the annals of Panthers history, and for good reason. The Panthers drafted Minter in the second round of the 1997 NFL Draft. He slotted in as a backup behind veteran Pat Terrell for the first five games of his rookie season before eventually taking over the starting gig. He would not relinquish that starting spot for the next ten years. Minter was a standout performer as a rookie, totaling 83 tackles, 3.5 sacks, and two fumble recoveries. His second season was derailed by a staph infection, but that was essentially the last thing that would keep Minter off the field for a very long time. He missed two games at the start of 2001, meaning he started 126 of 128 Panthers games between 1999 and 2006. Whenever he was on the field, he combined an intimidating physical presence over the middle of the field and around the line of scrimmage with the play making instincts to create turnovers. He finished his career with 17 interceptions, 12 forced fumbles, and 11 fumble recoveries. And his turnovers were more than changes of possession. He had a knack for picking up big yards on returns, He averaged nearly 25 yards per interception return and ran four of them back for touchdowns. Minter retired in 2007 due to lingering problems with his knee. He is top five in franchise history in tackles, forced fumbles, fumble recoveries, and interceptions. His 421 interception return yards is far and away the most in franchise history, nearly 100 more than second place. His four pick sixes are second only to Captain Munnerlyn’s five. Minter has stayed local since his retirement. He was a high school coach in Concord for a few years and was the head coach of Campbell University just south of Raleigh for 10 years. Mike Minter was by far the most impactful secondary player in the history of the Carolina Panthers. His name is all over the record books, and he truly embodied the play style of the Panthers in the 2007s. For that, he comes in at number 14 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

Okereke started 46 games over the last 3 seasons for the New York Giants, where he was fairly solid. summary: The Carolina Panthers have to cut their roster down from 90 to 53 by 6:00 PM ET on Sunday, August 30th. This is your live tracker and discussion thread for all of Carolina’s cuts this season. We will not be tracking notable cuts from other teams in this space. Any of those who get added […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - AUGUST 19: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers throws a pass during a joint training camp at Miller Electric Center on August 19, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have to cut their roster down from 90 to 53 by 6:00 PM ET on Sunday, August 30th. This is your live tracker and discussion thread for all of Carolina’s cuts this season. We will not be tracking notable cuts from other teams in this space. Any of those who get added to the Panthers will be addressed if and when they are signed. Keep in mind that the roster at 6 PM Sunday is not the same thing as the roster the Panthers will open with against the Chicago Bears on Sunday, September 9th. Late cuts can lead to adjustments through the rest of this week. NFL rules also make things difficult to deal with injured players at this time of year. Two players can be placed on injured reserve before final roster cuts and still be designated to return during the season. Any other player placed on injured reserve before 6 PM Sunday is ineligible to return this season. We’ll be watching Haynes King in particular with regards to his injury status this weekend. In short, expect things to change quickly and often, even after the deadline. With that in mind, stay tuned to this space. 2026 Roster Cuts Miles Davis, running back Tywone Malone, defensive tackle Caden Prieskorn, tight end Kyon Barrs, defensive tackle Elijah Cooks, wide receiver Roc Taylor, wide receiver Injury waivers and settlements Ryan Hayes, offensive tackle, waived-injured Dan Chisena, wide receiver, injury settlement (IR) Signings LB Bobby Okereke, Giants FanDuel odds for the playoffs Our friends at FanDuel are offering +250 odds for the Carolina Panthers to make the playoffs and -310 for them to miss them entirely. Roster cuts aren’t going to move that line all that much, but you can look to how many of other teams cast offs the Panthers pick up vs how many of their own cuts find jobs elsewhere in the league. On the one hand, this is the deepest roster the Panthers have fielded in a long time. That also means it has been a long time since other teams have had much interest in sniffing around the Panthers cuts. If teams pick up some of our soon-to-be-former guys then maybe the Panthers are in line for a brighter season than recent years would imply. If the Panthers are dumping their training camp players in favor of folks that couldn’t make an impact with another club then we can all expect more of the same. While it would be funny to back into the playoffs with a losing record for the second consecutive year, it would make for a necessarily stressful season. I think we’d all rather avoid that if possible. Checkout FanDuel , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation.

title: Panthers final 53 man roster prediction
summary: The preseason is done and over with for the Carolina Panthers. Now, teams have until 6:00pm Eastern on Sunday to trim their rosters from 90 players down to 53. We’ll make our best guess on what the final 53 is going to look like. On one hand, we already know the majority of the players […]
full_text: The preseason is done and over with for the Carolina Panthers. Now, teams have until 6:00pm Eastern on Sunday to trim their rosters from 90 players down to 53. We’ll make our best guess on what the final 53 is going to look like. On one hand, we already know the majority of the players since a lot of the roster has been pretty much set since the start of the offseason. On the other hand, on the bottom of the roster, there is a lot of movement left to happen, between practice squad assignments, injury designations, and waiver claims from other teams. Still, we’ll give it the old college try. Starters in bold and the order of players is a rough guess of the depth chart. Offense Quarterback (3) Bryce Young, Kenny Pickett, Haynes King I didn’t know what to do about King given that he hasn’t played since the Hall of Fame game, but it seems like Canales thinks he’ll be ready to play in Week 1 . That would imply that he would be on the roster. I think he’ll be comfortably behind the other two for standard quarterback play, but I wouldn’t be surprised if there are some packages for him to utilize his rushing ability. As for Young, everyone’s favorite conversation subject enters a make or break season as he tries to prove that he’s a legitimate starter in the NFL. Running back (3) Chuba Hubbard, Jonathon Brooks, Trevor Etienne/AJ Dillon (pending Etienne’s injury) The Panthers keep bringing competition in for Chuba Hubbard, and he keeps earning the starting spot. He’ll be the lead back to start the season, but Jonathon Brooks will push him for touches if he regains his college form. Etienne left Friday night’s game with an ankle injury, so his status is in flux. AJ Dillon may end up on the practice squad if Etienne’s injury is a mild one. Wide receiver (7) Tetairoa McMillan, Jalen Coker, Xavier Legette, Brycen Tremayne, Jimmy Horn Jr., John Metchie III, Ja’seem Reed Having Reed on here instead of David Moore might be more hope than prediction. Moore has been a reliable presence in the system for a couple of years and he brings value on special teams. Reed has shown a lot more as a receiver in camp and in the preseason, but Dan Morgan has said that special teams contributions weigh heavily in the decision making process at the bottom of the roster. I don’t know how Reed stacks up to Moore in that regard, but if it’s comparable, he can make the roster as the annual training camp wide receiver story. Metchie and Horn have been heavily featured in the preseason and have been appearing relatively early in the games, so it seems like they’re the highest among the second tier of wide receivers on the depth chart. Tremayne seems all but locked in as a good fill-in receiver and excellent special teams contributor. Tight End (3) Tommy Tremble, Mitchell Evans, Ja’Tavion Sanders The Panthers made a little bit of a splash signing Darren Waller, but his lack of appearances in the preseason make it seem like he’s not fully ready for game action. He can come up if and when the Panthers move on from Ja’Tavion Sanders, who seems like the odd man out at some point. There’s also James Mitchell hanging around, who’s one of those boring veterans that coaching staffs always love to have keeping things together. Feleipe Franks is also lurking as a special teams ace with some upside as an offensive player. Offensive Line (9) Rasheed Walker, Damien Lewis, Luke Fortner, Robert Hunt, Monroe Freeling , Brady Christensen, Sam Hecht, Chandler Zavala, Stone Forsythe The starting five is locked in while the Panthers wait for Ikem Ekwonu and Taylor Moton to return from their respective ailments. Fortner’s spot it by far the most tenuous, but I don’t think anyone is really pushing him to take the job right now. I know everyone would be excited to see Zavala back in the mix. Forsythe might be swapped out for Jake Curhan, but I’m not super well versed in how the backup tackle battle has been going in camp. Defense Defensive Line (5) Derrick Brown, Bobby Brown III, Cam Jackson, Lee Hunter, Jared Harrison-Hunte The last spot is up for grabs. Both Harrison-Hunte and Aaron Hall have made cases for themselves throughout camp and the preseason, and it seems like a coin flip as to who makes the roster. Whoever doesn’t make it is probably going straight to the practice squad if they clear waivers. Tershawn Wharton will also have some say in this group if and when he gets back from injury. Edge (5) Jaelan Phillips, Patrick Jones II, Princely Umanmielen, Trevis Gipson, Thomas Incoom Jaelan Phillips is the alpha in this group and Jones is the obvious number two after Nic Scourton went down for the season with a knee injury. Umanmielen has been looking good as a pass rusher in camp, while Gipson provides decent pop as depth and Incoom has a lot of special teams value. Cam Gill left a strong impression in the preseason finale with two fumble recoveries, but I don’t know if that’ll be enough to earn a spot on the final roster. Inside linebacker (5) Devin Lloyd, Trevin Wallace, Claudin Cherelus, Bam Martin-Scott, Jackson Kuwatch It’s sort of a make or break year for Wallace as a starter since he hasn’t quite developed at the rate the Panthers would be hoping for. He’ll get a huge upgrade starting alongside him in Devin Lloyd, and we’ll see if that helps him find his footing. The other three all bring value as special teams players, which is where we’ll see them for the vast majority of their snaps if the starters stay healthy. Cornerback (5) Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, Chau Smith-Wade, Will Lee, Akayleb Evans I wasn’t sure who to put in the final corner spot, but the fact that Evans was given the night off in the preseason finale would imply that he’s a safe bet to make the team unless there’s an injury we don’t know about. He’s got a role as a gunner on special teams and will probably only play corner in emergency situations. Chau Smith-Wade will play the nickel while Horn and Jackson reprise their roles as one of the best corner duos in the league. Safety (5) Tre’von Moehrig, Nick Scott , Lathan Ransom, Zakee Wheatley, Isaiah Simmons Five safeties is a lot of safeties, but Simmons is really more a special teams player than a true safety. Moehrig is firmly entrenched as a very good starter, while Scott is likely to be pushed for reps by the young guys Ransom and Wheatley. Specialists (3) Kicker: Ryan Fitzgerald Punter: Sam Martin Long snapper: JJ Jansen No surprises here. None of the three have even gotten competition in camp. The Panthers will be rolling with the same trio as last season.

summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: Football: Jacksonville Jaguars offensive lineman Richard Collier (76) in action vs Carolina Panthers Mike Rucker (93). Jacksonville, FL 12/9/2007 CREDIT: Steve Jacobson (Photo by Steve Jacobson /Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #15. Mike Rucker Mike Rucker was an elite complementary defensive end. It might be a disservice to call him that, but that’s kind of what he was simply due to the sheer talent alongside him for much of his time in Carolina. The Panthers drafted Rucker in the second round of the 1999 NFL Draft. He played in a rotational role for his first two seasons and accumulated 5.5 sacks in that time. After the retirement of Reggie White, Rucker slid in to the starting defensive end spot opposite Jay Williams. He was the best pass rusher on the team that season, leading the group with nine sacks as the team struggled to a 1-15 record. That putrid season allowed the team to draft Julius Peppers, and he and Rucker formed one of the most formidable edge duos in the league with monsters on the interior like Kris Jenkins making the entire front four a nightmare for the rest of the league. Rucker hit double digit sacks in each of his first two seasons opposite Peppers. His sack production dipped in the subsequent seasons, but he was still a very effective player as an edge setter and all around solid defensive end. He tore his ACL near the end of the 2006 season. He was able to rehab in time to return for the 2007 season, and despite quickly regaining his pre-injury form, he decided to call it a career after that season at the age of 33. Rucker amassed 55.5 sacks in his time in Carolina, good for third in franchise history behind Peppers and Charles Johnson. He was also credited with two safeties, which is tied for the most in Panthers history. He never suited up for another team and has remained connected with the franchise and the city of Charlotte since his retirement; he called Panthers preseason games on local TV for a number of years. He’s a Carolina Panther through and through, For that, and for his time and effectiveness on the field as a Panther, he earns spot number 15 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Bears vs Titans: Inside the snap counts, stats, and an injury update
summary: The Chicago Bears’ backups beat the Tennessee Titans’ backups last night, 24 to 15, and the NFL is done with the preseason games, so bring on Week 1 and the Carolina Panthers! The Bears had more yards (398 to 259), more first downs (19 to 13), and led in time of possession (35:44 to 24:16). […]
full_text: Aug 29, 2026; Nashville, Tennessee, USA; Chicago Bears running back Roschon Johnson (23) celebrates with wide receiver Zavion Thomas (81) after scoring a touchdown against the Tennessee Titans during the third quarter at Nissan Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Chicago Bears’ backups beat the Tennessee Titans’ backups last night, 24 to 15, and the NFL is done with the preseason games, so bring on Week 1 and the Carolina Panthers! The Bears had more yards (398 to 259), more first downs (19 to 13), and led in time of possession (35:44 to 24:16). The Bears also converted 4 of 5 fourth-down attempts, while the Titans converted their only 4th-down try. Chicago was also better on third downs: 6-15 (40.0%) to 3-11 (27.3%). The Bears were flagged 10 times for 71 yards to Tennessee’s 7 for 46 yards. In his postgame press conference, head coach Ben Johnson said that running back Brittain Brown left the game with a concussion, and that cornerback Jaylon Jones and wideout Ray-Ray McCloud III had hamstring injuries. He also said that left tackle Ozzy Trapilo, who has yet to practice in full since being taken off the PUP list, is “right on track.” He also said that wide receiver Luther Burden III “looks 100% to me.” Patrick Finley of the Chicago Sun-Times shared that before the game, starting corner Jaylon Johnson, “who left practice Thursday after appearing to hurt his right arm/shoulder, is doing rehab work in the end zone, throwing a heavy ball and using stretching bands.” Running back Salvon Ahmed was kept out of the game with a minor injury, per Brad Biggs of the Chicago Tribune. Before we get into some more numbers, here are all the Bears who did not play against the Titans. And here is how the Bears started the day on both sides of the ball. Here are the Bears’ playing time breakdowns and a few individual stats. Offense Tyson Bagent played the entire first half, and he went 16 of 17 for 208 yards, 2 touchdowns, and a passer rating of 156.9, with 2 runs for 21 yards. He was credited with a fumble on a bad exchange with rookie Zavion Thomas on a jet sweep, but in his postgame presser, Thomas took full responsibility for it. Zavion had 5 catches for a game-high 140 yards, a 97-yard TD on the first play from the offense, plus a 39-yard kick return and a 22-yard punt return. Roschon Johnson led the Bears in rushing with 15 attempts, 52 yards, and a TD. Wideout Maurice Alexander led the Bears with 7 receptions for 50 yards and a TD. He also filled in at tailback when Brown left with a concussion, and he had 11 yards on 3 carries. Defense Rookie linebacker Wayne Matthews III led the defense with 6 tackles. Linebacker T.J. Edwards, one of the few starters for the Bears who played, had 5 tackles. Defensive end Jamree Kromah had 3 tackles, a tackle for loss, and a sack. UDFA defensive tackle Jayden Loving had 2 tackles, 2 TFLs, a sack, a forced fumble, and a pass defended. Corner Terell Smith had 2 passes defended. Special Teams *The above image has players who only played in the third phase. Cairo Santos was 3 for 3 on extra points, and he hit his only field goal (from 37). Tory Taylor had 2 punts and a 56 average (56 net), with 1 punt inside the twenty. Linebacker Antonio Grier, who was just signed this week, had 3 special teams tackles plus 3 more on defense. To check out the full Bears vs. Titans box score, ESPN has an easy-to-navigate site. All statistics, snap counts, and accompanying pictures are taken directly from the NFL’s Game Statistics and Information System.

title: Notes: Bears close out preseason with strong win
summary: The Bears closed out their 2026 preseason on a high note, heading to Tennessee and defeating the Titans in a 24-15 matchup. The win on Saturday gave them a 2-1 record to close out the preseason, bumping Ben Johnson’s career record in the preseason to 4-1-1 over his two seasons as Chicago’s head coach. There’s […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 29: Tyson Bagent #17 of the Chicago Bears drops back to pass during the first half of Week 3 preseason game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Bears closed out their 2026 preseason on a high note, heading to Tennessee and defeating the Titans in a 24-15 matchup. The win on Saturday gave them a 2-1 record to close out the preseason, bumping Ben Johnson’s career record in the preseason to 4-1-1 over his two seasons as Chicago’s head coach. There’s only so much worth taking away from a preseason game, and while very few concrete conclusions can be made from these games, it’s still exciting to see Bears football back on television. It’s also been fun to watch some of their young players thriving in spurts and showing signs of what they could become in the NFL. After a few years doing the instant recaps for WCG, I’m excited to be back working on the day-after notes. These are some of my takeaways from Saturday’s preseason finale for the Bears. The Zavion Thomas game After missing the first two preseason games due to injury, third-round wide receiver Zavion Thomas made his Bears preseason on Saturday. His first glimpse of NFL action was incredibly encouraging, as he caught five passes for 140 receiving yards and a touchdown. He also provided some of that high-level returning skill he demonstrated in his collegiate stints with Mississippi State and LSU, returning a punt back 39 yards. Though the Bears followed the return up with a turnover on downs, his return set them up in a favorable position to begin the drive. In particular, Thomas scored a 97-yard touchdown on a stop-and-go off a pass from Tyson Bagent. It was an impressive debut from the rookie, as he showed off the elite speed that was a major calling card of his game in college. He had some rocky production in college, as his 77.4 PFN WR Impact Score ranked just No. 106 in the FBS last season. That said, his elite athleticism shined in spurts at LSU, and his upside as a big-play weapon for Ben Johnson’s offense showed up in how well he played on Saturday. As someone who was (and, to an extent, still is) skeptical about taking him in the third round, I’m certainly intrigued. Tyson Bagent looks surgical After missing Week 2 of the preseason, Tyson Bagent started at quarterback for the Bears against the Titans on Saturday. He played the entire first half in the preseason finale, and after an inconsistent first outing against the Browns, he dominated against Tennessee. He completed 16 of his 17 passing attempts, demonstrating the floor-general archetype of surgical distribution with underneath passes. Between the two games he played this preseason, Bagent combined going 30-for-40 with a 75.0% completion percentage, 382 passing yards, three passing touchdowns, and an interception for a 119.0 passer rating. This marks the third year in a row that he finished with a passer rating above 100.0 in the preseason, which shows just how tremendous he’s been when given an opportunity. Terell Smith making some plays in coverage Another player who made his only preseason appearance on Saturday was Terell Smith, the fourth-year cornerback who missed the entirety of the 2025 season due to injury. He certainly looked the part against the Titans, deflecting each of the two targets he faced in coverage. The 6’0”, 207-pound cornerback looked sticky in 21 snaps of coverage. The Bears saw plenty of chaotic play out of their secondary last year, and though losing Jaylon Johnson and Kyler Gordon for much of the regular season certainly hurt, it also didn’t help that Smith missed the whole year as arguably their top backup cornerback. Having him available as a depth option should be a big benefit for Chicago going into 2026. The rookies look good Between the Bears’ three preseason matchups, they were fortunate enough to see some bright flashes from the players they selected in the 2026 NFL Draft. Dillon Thieneman got under a deep ball and broke up a pass that could’ve resulted in a touchdown against the Titans. Thomas had his aforementioned breakout game. Sam Roush caught five passes for 64 yards, not dropping any of his targets across three games. Logan Jones had some ups and downs, but he displayed good quickness off the line of scrimmage and a strong anchor in pass protection at center. There was also a learning curve from Malik Muhammad moving inside from his usual perimeter alignment, but he looked sound in zone coverage underneath. And though he was more quiet on Saturday than he was in his first two preseason games, Jordan van den Berg still looked disruptive along the defensive interior. Like I said earlier, you can’t make any concrete conclusions out of these preseason games, but Chicago has to feel pretty good about the early returns it’s getting out of its rookie class.

title: NFL Waiver Wire Rules: Chicago Bears are 25th
summary: The 32 NFL teams will let go of over a thousand players when the 2026 preseason wraps up, as they’ll all get their 90-man offseason rosters down to 53 active players for the regular season. That deadline is 5:00 pm (CT) on Sunday, but teams aren’t waiting til them to notify their players. The Chicago […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 10: General view of a Chicago Bears helmet prior to a preseason game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on August 10, 2024 in Orchard Park, New York. The Bears won 33-6. (Photo by Rich Barnes/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 32 NFL teams will let go of over a thousand players when the 2026 preseason wraps up, as they’ll all get their 90-man offseason rosters down to 53 active players for the regular season. That deadline is 5:00 pm (CT) on Sunday, but teams aren’t waiting til them to notify their players. The Chicago Bears and Tennessee Titans were the last two teams playing this preseason, so some of the other clubs have already started making moves. We’ll certainly hear about some Bears being let go by the morning, and when they are, you can stay abreast of all the transactions in our tracker right here . The Bears hope they get the right combination of players to help them repeat as division champs for the first time since the 2005 and 2006 seasons. Our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook have the Bears with the third-best odds to win the NFC North at +330. But before they get there, they have a lot of transactions to make to get ready for Week 1, and that starts with cut-down day. Released players around the League become street free agents and can sign with any team, but waived players must go through waivers. What’s the difference? Vested veterans are players with four or more credited seasons of NFL experience, and when they are released, they are not subject to waivers. They can immediately negotiate with teams. The NFLPA defines a credited season as being on the active, inactive, injured reserve, or PUP list for three or more regular-season or post-season NFL games, or if a player is released injured and receives an injury settlement or grievance for the equivalent of 3 or more regular-season games. Players with less than four credited seasons are waived and subject to waivers. If these players go unclaimed, they are free to negotiate with teams as free agents or for a practice squad job. When is the waiver deadline? After all 32 teams file their transactions with the NFL (by 5 pm (CT) on Sunday), they’ll have until Noon (CT) on August 31 to file their claims. The League will review those claims and then announce which claims were successful. A claimed player will need a corresponding roster move to make room on the roster. That player, if waived, will be on waivers the next day. Once those transactions are announced, teams can officially start filling their 16-man practice squads with unclaimed players or street free agents. What is the current waiver order? It’s last year’s NFL Draft order before trades. Las Vegas Raiders New York Jets Arizona Cardinals Tennessee Titans New York Giants Cleveland Browns Washington Commanders New Orleans Saints Kansas City Chiefs Cincinnati Bengals Miami Dolphins Dallas Cowboys Atlanta Falcons Baltimore Ravens Tampa Bay Buccaneers Indianapolis Colts Detroit Lions Minnesota Vikings Carolina Panthers Green Bay Packers Pittsburgh Steelers Los Angeles Chargers Philadelphia Eagles Jacksonville Jaguars Chicago Bears Buffalo Bills San Francisco 49ers Houston Texans Los Angeles Rams Denver Broncos New England Patriots Seattle Seahawks This waiver order will stay this way for the first three weeks of the season; after that, it’ll go from worst to first based on the teams’ current standings each subsequent week. How many players can a team claim? There’s no limit, really, as technically, the Raiders could put in a claim for 53 new players. That’ll never happen, but each team lists who they want, and the waivers process in order. So the Raiders will get all the players they claim. If there’s anyone left on the Jets list, they’ll be awarded them. If everyone the Cardinals listed is gone, the waivers move to the Titans, and this goes on through all 32 teams. Every team that wins a claim must release a player; and if that player is vested, he’s an immediate free agent, but if not, he’s placed on waivers, and the whole process begins again the next day for the waived players.

Teams need to be compliant by 5:00 pm (CT) on Sunday, August 30. Yes, tomorrow! That means by this time tomorrow we’ll know who the initial 53-man roster for the Chicago Bears’ 2026 season will be, and the quest for Super Bowl LXI is on! Our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook have the Bears odds to win it all at +2700, the 16th-best. Here are a few things to keep in mind as the Bears get down to 53. Players with fewer than four credited seasons will go through waivers, and once players clear waivers — this year’s waiver deadline is Monday, August 31 at Noon (CT) — they are eligible to be signed to a team’s 16-man practice squad. A 17th practice squad spot is available if the player qualifies and is designated as an International Player. We have all the specifics on the waiver wire process here . We’ll launch our practice squad tracker on Sunday. If a club has a player on the Active/Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list — the Bears have three such players — or the Active/Non-Football Injury or Illness (NFI) list, then they must select one of the following options: Move the player to the Reserve/PUP or Reserve/NFI, whichever is applicable, and any player on the Reserve PUP or NFI list will need to remain there for at least 4 games Terminate or request waivers with the designation of a failed physical or NFI, whichever is applicable Request waivers Terminate the contract Trade the player Take him off the list and add him to the active 53-man roster Teams are also permitted to place up to two players on injured reserve at the 5:00 pm deadline. Those players will be sidelined for at least 4 games, with up to eight players eligible to be designated to return (10 if the team makes the playoffs). Any player put on IR before the cut-down deadline will be ineligible to play the entire season. The Bears currently have 4 such players. We’ll track all the Bears’ cuts and transactions here: The Bears have traded Gervon Dexter Sr. to the Atlanta Falcons for a 5th-round pick and cornerback Clark Phillips III. summary: With just two weeks to go until the regular season, the Chicago Bears appear to be a very offensive-loaded football team. A 2025 defense that gave up the fourth-most yards per game and fifth-most passing touchdowns per game parted ways with three main starters (among other key players) in the offseason, and the Bears still […]
full_text: Co-owner Steve Cusano uses a crowbar to smash a computer screen in The Relief Room on Tuesday, March 19, 2019 in Malta, N.Y. The business is a so-called "rage room," where people pay so they can don protective gear and smash up office and household items to relieve their stress. It is the first of its kind in the area. (Photo by Lori Van Buren/Albany Times Union via Getty Images) With just two weeks to go until the regular season, the Chicago Bears appear to be a very offensive-loaded football team. A 2025 defense that gave up the fourth-most yards per game and fifth-most passing touchdowns per game parted ways with three main starters (among other key players) in the offseason, and the Bears still drafted three offensive players in the first three rounds of the 2026 draft. Continued success on the offensive line, a (fingers crossed) healthy receiving group, and another step forward developmentally by quarterback Caleb Williams are good bets to make them confident they can win shootouts. Speaking of Caleb Williams, he broke his way into the top-10 conversation for fantasy projections, with both CBS and Fantasy Pros ranking him in the single digits, and ESPN ranking him as the 11th-best projected quarterback. His other-wordly ability to extend plays bodes well for quarterback rushing stats when nobody breaks open late, and his 11.9 yards-per-completed pass ranked 5th among qualified quarterbacks in 2025. Much was made about his lackluster completion percentage, but it’s a problem that will have ripple effects if it gets corrected. After parting with receiver DJ Moore in the offseason, the Bears enter this season with a clear trio of pass catchers. Tight end Colston Loveland broke out in the second half of the season, catching all 6 of his touchdowns in weeks 9-16. It’s likely his target share will only grow as Ben Johnson and the coaching staff figure out new ways to scheme him open, and expect him to open the season better than he did last. He’ll be a top-5 tight end in your fantasy draft. Rome Odunze is entering his third year as a receiver for the Bears. A foot injury derailed an incredible start to last season where he led the league in touchdown catches through the first month. He described the lingering effects of that injury as his “ new normal ” before clarifying that phrasing later , but he’ll still probably be around later in most drafts than some may expect. Luther Burden, on the other hand, has been getting a lot of attention as a potential breakout candidate this season. He hauled in 47 passes in 2025 despite just about a 13% target share , so while some may look to Odunze as profiting the most in the post-DJ Moore Bears offense, it’s probably going to be Burden.
