title: Broncos vs Vikings: The No Bull Preseason Review
summary: I always dread the final preseason game of each season. We get decent backups for less than a half, typically, then it is just a bunch of dudes who won’t make the team passing the time by and large. I will say that I sure do prefer seeing the good guys drop a 30-burger on […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - AUGUST 28: Jarrett Stidham #8 of the Denver Broncos looks to pass during the first quarter against the Minnesota Vikings in a preseason game at Empower Field at Mile High on August 28, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images I always dread the final preseason game of each season. We get decent backups for less than a half, typically, then it is just a bunch of dudes who won’t make the team passing the time by and large. I will say that I sure do prefer seeing the good guys drop a 30-burger on the opponents while the defense holds them to under 10 points. The Broncos gave their roster a lot of great chances to make a showing for the coaching staff. That’s going to sadly be muddied a bit by the Vikings’ depth not playing well enough to do the same. I’m going to switch up the format here and talk about each group collectively instead of deep dives on players other than the players who really stood out. This will allow us to talk about cut downs and what roster decisions need to be made, which seems more apropos for reviewing this game. Offense Davis Webb ran the offense through a lot of really basic concepts for the Broncos offense. Most of it worked. Blown coverages led to big scores. This game offensively should really help the team make final decisions on their roster depth. There were some question marks at running back and wide receivers that got some quality snaps for the coaching staff to look at and see if they want to, as Sean Payton put it, “turn their chairs.” Quarterbacks Jarret Stidham has the backup quarterback position on lock. The only question for the quarterback room is whether or not the team needs to keep a roster spot for Sam Ehlinger. While Ehlinger did stand out on paper, I’d put a big asterisk by his stat line. Two of his touchdowns were on completely busted coverages, which are looks that he wouldn’t see against a normal quality NFL defense. So while those of Broncos Country in the stands may get hyped for him, my take is the same. He’s a decent enough backup guy, but solidly behind Stidham in my mind. I’d still not save a roster spot for him. Let him go through waivers and come back to the practice squad. If another team takes him, so be it. We can pick up another practice squad #3 QB and get them trained up. Line What I liked about the offensive line in this game was that they blocked well in both the passing game and running game throughout the game. That allowed me to focus on the interesting battles (because I didn’t think there was any real battle happening on the line anyway). I think the only interesting question for our line is what the center’s health looks like going into week 1 of the season. What we all want to see is both Alex Forsyth and Luke Wattenburg healthy. That we got to see snaps from Wattenburg has me feeling good about being ready for the Chiefs in week 1. Running Backs This is where things get interesting to me. Of the guys I’m thinking are not set heading into the season, we got to see a battle between Tyler Badie, Jaleel McLaughlin, and Cody Schrader. While all three of them saw plenty of snaps, we got a show put on by Cody Schrader. Schrader finished the game with 13 runs for 42 yards, including a long of 12. He caught 6 passes for 90 yards and a touchdown as well. He also got some work in the blocking game and really impressed. The question becomes: is one game of wow enough? I think it may be when it comes to the decision between him and Jaleel McLaughlin. McLaughlin did have 6 runs for 24 yards and got 6 catches for 35 yards with a long of 20 and a touchdown. That’s very comparable, but the difference is that we already know that McLaughlin doesn’t pass block as well. He also doesn’t contribute to special teams. I think Tyler Badie is a lock because of how good he is as a blocker out of the backfield and his versatility to be consistent if they ask him to run or pass as a depth back. I think McLaughlin is a candidate for trade. He’s a very good runner who can produce if you can block up holes for him. In other schemes, I think he might be a very decent #2 RB on a team. I think Schrader is a lock on the team as a practice squad player. I believe you can chance the waiver wire with him; if some other team claims him, they probably were mesmerized by one game vs scrubs. Receivers From the WR room, Troy Franklin got a couple of forced targets early and didn’t complete either (though to be fair to him, the first one was a bad throw by Stidham). Michael Bandy had a few targets and will likely be available for the practice squad again. Dane Key had a very good catch down the sideline for 26 yards. Cameron Ross only had one catch for 6 yards, but I honestly love what I’ve seen from him so far in preseason action and training camp and think he makes the practice squad as well. Our tight ends got some work as well. Nate Adkins got a 26-yard reception on a crossing route off bootleg play action and a 10-yard catch in the red zone. Justin Joly had an 88-yard catch for a touchdown alone on one half of the field deep. Defense Vance Joseph lit a fire under the defense this week. They were far more dialed in than what we saw last week vs the Packers. I thought the scheme just looked tighter than what we saw last week. Most catches that were made were just really good throws and not uncontested. The run game was also well defended outside of a handful of runs later in the game. We saw the team rallying well to the ball and keeping things fairly contained. Front 7 I liked what we saw for the future of the inside linebacker position. There were a lot of competitive snaps from Karene Reid (led the team in tackles), Red Murdock (forced a fumble), Jordan Turner (got a quarterback hit on a pressure), and Taurean York. We’re going to see Reid and Murdock on the roster week one. Que Robinson has the Broncos willing and able to miss Jonathan Cooper in week 1. He created pressure to force throwaways and consistently is able to get up the field from the outside. Cooper, per usual, is a bull rush monster. The Broncos will likely use Jonah Ellis if he misses time, who has shown better ability to set the edge vs the rush. Secondary The biggest points I’ve got to make in the secondary were that Kris Abrams-Draine didn’t get beat like a drum this week and J.L. Skinner looks like our backup safety at the moment (barring the Broncos bringing back Taylor Rapp). Parker Robinson did get a ton of work and accounted well for himself in this game. He had 4 tackles on the day with a tackle for loss and a fumble recovery. I’d love to see the young safety stick around on the practice squad. Special Teams Colby Katsis has flashed multiple times in the preseason in the return game. He had a 49-yard return off a great cut to find daylight that had everyone hyped. This guy may be the insurance policy the Broncos have in case Marvin Mims pops off this year and gets lost to free agency next offseason. Devon Key got absolutely ole’d at the sideline, whiffing on a tackle. That’s not the kind of film you want to put out there as a depth guy on special teams. Final Thoughts We’ll be watching cuts happen as the roster gets finalized. This game doesn’t represent much of any meaning for what the Broncos will look like in Week 1. The players playing that week, by and large, didn’t even play in this game. Given the state of this team, it is very hard for young players to be relied on for a team that is in the running for a deep playoff run. This is a veteran team. Sean Payton needs players on the roster who can consistently contribute to winning football games. Good luck to all the young players who played in this game and wore the orange and blue for the Broncos. We’ll be cheering for you and hoping for success for all of you in your future! title: NFL waiver wire rules and order
summary: NFL cut day is this Sunday by 4:00 pm MT. All NFL teams will trim their rosters down to 53 players. One interesting mechanic that comes into play is the waiver process. Let’s cover the rules so that Broncos Country knows how it works, why the Broncos may use it, and how their success this […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - AUGUST 14: Cody Schrader #25 of the Denver Broncos rushes during the fourth quarter against the Atlanta Falcons in an NFL preseason game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images NFL cut day is this Sunday by 4:00 pm MT. All NFL teams will trim their rosters down to 53 players. One interesting mechanic that comes into play is the waiver process. Let’s cover the rules so that Broncos Country knows how it works, why the Broncos may use it, and how their success this season will impact their priority in the future. When Waivers Come Into Play From operations.nfl.com : “When a player contract is terminated, he is either free to negotiate and (sign) with a team at any time or subject to waivers. When released, a contract for a player with fewer than four credited seasons is subject to waivers at all times.” The biggest influx of players in the waiver system is on cut day. The vast majority of players that are waived by the team they’ve gone through training camp with are going to be players with fewer than four credited seasons. This means almost every Tom, Dick, and Harry that teams cut could be claimed by other teams. What Happens When Teams Claim A Player Again, from operations.nfl.com : “The waiver system allows teams to place a claim on a player contract before that player becomes a free agent. The team with the highest priority will be awarded the player.” The order of priority for the 32 teams follows the draft order of the previous season (basically, the worst record gets the first pick, with the last priority going to the team with the best record). Playoff teams automatically get seeded into the list in order of worst record to best after all the other non-playoff teams in the list. So when a player is cut by a team, any other team can put in a waiver for that player. If no other team puts in a claim, the team gets the player directly. If two or more teams put in a claim, the team with the highest priority (read: worst record) gets the player. Ties are broken by the worst strength of schedule. Broncos Waiver Wire The Denver Broncos should currently sit at #30 on the waiver priority list (after week 4, teams will be reshuffled according to their record). This is based on their season record last year of 14-3 and their success in the playoffs, taking them to the AFC Championship game. Good teams get less opportunity to pick up players who make it to the waiver system. According to FanDuel , the odds say the Broncos win 9.5 total games this season, which would give them a much higher pecking order next season when players get waived… but Broncos Country knows we’re taking the over on that line. One area the Broncos could utilize the waiver system would be their offensive line, especially at center. The depth with our #1 and #2 center options injured has been less than impressive, and we may need a competent snapper to help until our starter(s) get healthy. title: 2026 Detroit Lions final roster bubble predictions on defense
summary: The Detroit Lions have a ton of decisions to make on Sunday afternoon, as the deadline to get to roster to 53 players is 6 p.m. ET. And, personally, I believe most of the tough decisions are on the defensive side of the ball. That’s highlighted by our final edition of 2026 Detroit Lions Bubble […]
full_text: Defensive end Levi Onwuzurike practices during minicamp at Detroit Lions headquarters and practice facility in Allen Park on Tuesday, June 4, 2024. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions have a ton of decisions to make on Sunday afternoon, as the deadline to get to roster to 53 players is 6 p.m. ET. And, personally, I believe most of the tough decisions are on the defensive side of the ball. That’s highlighted by our final edition of 2026 Detroit Lions Bubble Watch, where our staff makes their predictions for which players are in, and who is out. Before we get into our defensive selections, you can catch up on other roster construction predictions below: Final Detroit Lions roster bubble predictions on offense Final Detroit Lions 53-man roster prediction: Erik Schlitt Final Detroit Lions 53-man roster prediction: Jeremy Reisman View Link Defensive end : Assumed in: Aidan Hutchinson, DJ Wonnum, Derrick Moore Off Bubble Watch: Payton Turner (IR) Ahmed Hassanein: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Anthony Lucas: 0 votes (no change) Eric O’Neill: 0 votes (no change) Despite a very strong preseason finale—producing three pressures—Eric O’Neill didn’t garner a vote from our staff. I think he has a chance to make the roster given how disruptive he’s been in the last few weeks, but it is very hard to find room for him. Defensive tackle: Assumed in: Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams Tyler Lacy: 11 votes (no change) Skyler Gill-Howard: 11 votes (no change) Levi Onwuzurike: 9 votes (down 2) Chris Smith: 9 votes (down 1) Ben Stille: 3 votes (up 3) Mekhi Wingo: 1 vote (up 1) Tyre West: 0 votes (no change) Lacy and Gill-Howard have seemingly locked down roster spots behind McNeill and Williams. But where the Lions go for that DT5 and possibly DT6 spots remains very up in the air. Ben Stille is making a late push despite a quiet preseason finale that featured just 10 snaps. However, he has been a constant force in training camp and received some high praise from Campbell this week when asked about the veteran defender. “He’s a pro, smart, really smart. He’s got versatility, strong, very strong,” Campbell said. “He can shed blocks, shock, shed, make plays, kind of knows himself, knows what he is, knows his own limitations, and can play fast enough to cover up for some of those. But that’s what’s the intrigue with him is the versatility, man. He can play some big end, we think; he can play the nose, certainly, and then three if you needed it. So the more you can do and the more that you can prove you can do, that is always going to help your case.” He garnered three votes, which came directly from Levi Onwuzurike (down two votes) and Chris Smith (down one). Onwuzurike is a tough nut to crack, because he’s been getting reps anywhere from the starters to the third team in practice, and just about every time it looks like he’s finally returning to form, he goes missing for a large portion of practice or games. Smith is a known commodity, and his spot on the roster is essentially contingent on what the Lions want in their depth. Smith is a relatively limited player in terms of versatility (a nose tackle), but he’s also pretty darn good at it. Linebacker: Assumed in: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez Off bubble watch: Damone Clark (IR) Devin White: 11 votes (no change) Trevor Nowaske: 11 votes (up 1) Jimmy Rolder: 4 votes (down 4) Joe Bachie: 4 votes (up 4) Troy Reeder: 1 vote (no change) Erick Hunter: 0 votes (no change) Once again, our staff is split when it comes down to getting beyond LB5. Nowaske, despite dealing with a minor injury, has locked down that fifth spot, but decisions await after that. Nine of our 11 staff have the Lions keeping a sixth linebacker, but that decision hinges on what Detroit does with Jimmy Rolder. The fourth-round rookie is still sidelined with a leg injury, and he’s missed most of camp. But all signs point to him being able to return imminently, especially when he revealed a week ago that he thought he may be able to practice in the final week of training camp. But Campbell poured cold water on that last week, and Rolder never returned to practice. Does that mean he’s headed for a start on the IR to save a roster spot and delay his development? Or will he make the 53-man roster and start practicing right away? Our staff can’t seem to come to a consensus. Cornerback: Assumed in: DJ Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Keith Abney Ennis Rakestraw: 11 votes (no change) Nick Whiteside: 11 votes (no change) Roger McCreary: 11 votes (no change) Khalil Dorsey: 9 votes (no change) No changes were made this week by our staff, but there were some interesting developments. For one, Khalil Dorsey did not play in the final preseason game. Is that a sign of his roster spot being safe as one of the team’s best special teamers, or did the Lions simply want to get more playing time for the rest of the reserves? Additionally, Ennis Rakestraw continued his up-and-down preseason with a couple of allowed catches, followed by a big interception. None of that changed our opinion, and it will be interesting to see how many cornerbacks the Lions end up keeping, especially if you consider Christian Izien a nickel. Safety Assumed in: Christian Izien, Avonte Maddox, Chuck Clark Thomas Harper: 11 votes (no change) Dan Jackson: 0 votes (no change) Brian Branch: 0 votes (no change) Kerby Joseph: 0 votes (no change) New to roster bubble: Aamaris Brown (0 votes) Speaking of Izien, we’re not 100 percent clear on his Week 1 status, nor do we know if Avonte Maddox is dealing with something serious after suffering an apparent injury on the final play of training camp. With no new information to work with, no one moved off their mark. However, I did add Aamaris Brown to the roster bubble for two reasons. One, I thought he played outstandingly in the preseason finale. And two, because of all the unknown injury situations at the position, it’s possible he could squeak his way onto the roster.

Tight end: Assumed in: Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright Tyler Conklin: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Jackson Meeks: 9 votes (no change) Thomas Gordon: 0 votes (no change) Meeks had another fairly strong outing in the preseason finale, but he didn’t seem to change anyone’s mind on the staff. He’s very much one of the last players in or out depending on your perspective, but kudos to him for making it a serious conversation despite still very much learning the nuances of the tight end position. Offensive tackle: Assumed in: Penei Sewell, Blake Miller, Larry Borom Colby Sorsdal: 0 votes (no change) Devin Cochran: 0 votes (no change) It would be a pretty big shock if the Lions’ offensive tackle room looked any different than this. The entire Lions offensive line looked strong against the Colts, so it’s possible someone like Devin Cochran gets consideration, but that feels much more likely to be a practice squad add. Interior offensive line: Assumed in: Tate Ratledge, Christian Mahogany, Miles Frazier Assumed on IR: Cade Mays Juice Scruggs: 11 votes (no change) Ben Bartch: 11 votes (up 1) Seth McLaughlin: 5 votes (down 3) Michael Niese: 0 votes (no change) New to bubble watch: Mason Miller: 0 votes Scruggs is a lock as the Week 1 starter, and Ben Bartch—who was initially considered a serious contender for the starting left guard job—likely has secured a job by simply remaining healthy for over a week. The staff is currently split evenly, with Seth McLaughlin being the only reserve to garner an OL9 vote—he got five. That said, I do wonder if the Lions will consider Mason Miller after the week he had. With no center experience, he backfilled for McLaughlin (who was in concussion protocol), and besides an understandable snap exchange issue or two, was pretty remarkable. “I was proud of Mason Miller,” Campbell said after the game. “He has not played at center […] but we worked him all week at center, we were going to give him the start, and minus the—we had one quarterback, center exchange (issue)—man, I thought he played pretty dang clean. title: What is the Detroit Lions’ toughest 53-man roster decision?
summary: Welcome to the worst day on the entire NFL calendar. On Sunday, by 6 p.m. ET, all 32 NFL teams must shave their roster down to 53 players. For teams that carried 90 men for months, that means ending the dreams of 37 players per team—or 1,184 people losing their jobs. Sure, nearly half of […]
full_text: Aug 29, 2026; Indianapolis, Indiana, USA; Detroit Lions tight end Jackson Meeks (13) celebrates with teammates after a play against the Indianapolis Colts during the first half at Lucas Oil Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Robert Goddin-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to the worst day on the entire NFL calendar. On Sunday, by 6 p.m. ET, all 32 NFL teams must shave their roster down to 53 players. For teams that carried 90 men for months, that means ending the dreams of 37 players per team—or 1,184 people losing their jobs. Sure, nearly half of them (512) will find haven on a practice squad and another handful may find a spot on another team’s 53-man roster, but it will still be a tough pill for those players to swallow. It’s never easy to hear that you didn’t do enough or you’re not good enough. I don’t care what size your paycheck is. Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell has constantly said he abhors this day, and I can’t imagine it’s much easier for general manager Brad Holmes. “It’s something that has to be done, and you want to do it as respectfully as you can,” Campbell said last year. “You don’t want to lie to the player, you just tell them straight up, and it’s hard. But it’s the right way to do it.” As the years go on and the roster gets deeper, cut down decisions get harder. So today’s Question of the Day is: What is the Lions’ toughest decision for the 53-man roster? My answer: I’ll give you three. TE Jackson Meeks I don’t quite think Meeks is ready to get significant time as a tight end. He’s obviously a decent receiving option with his wide receiver background, but his blocking remains a work in progress. That said, I’ve personally witnessed growth there, and given his tenacity on special teams, I found a way to put him on my final 53-man roster projections . Still, a developmental TE4 feels like a bit of a luxury, and I don’t think he would have any issue clearing waivers and continuing his development on the practice squad. Eric O’Neill vs. Chris Smith vs. Levi Onwuzurike vs. Ben Stille Campbell could not stop talking about how deep the Lions’ defensive tackle room is all training camp. “The d-line room is, I mean, that can go any way right now, it really can,” Campbell said this week. “I mean, there’s a number of guys in there, the hard thing is you can’t keep all those guys. You just can’t, not without it hurting the rest of your roster. And there are some good players in there and there’s some veterans, there’s some young guys, there’s raw talent, but there’s things in there that you really like.” Personally, I was only able to find room for two of the above four: Smith and Stille. For me, Stille and Onwuzurike are fighting for one spot, as each have the versatility to play anywhere from the nose to the big end spot. Stille, in my opinion, was just better and more consistent all camp. As someone who came in with a lot of hope for Onwuzurike, this is not a decision I take lightly, and I truly do hope his career rebounds after everything he’s been through. O’Neill vs. Smith was just a debate of where the Lions want their depth. Do you invest in a young, promising pass rusher or keep a reliable, veteran run stuffer? They’re two very different roles, but I stuck with the veteran because of how much this team still values stopping the run. Flashy pass rushers in the summer come and go (see: Isaac Ukwu, Nate Lynn, etc.), and I think O’Neill needs to expand his game to land on the 53-man roster. That said, he certainly made plays on a daily basis, and I wouldn’t bat an eye if he made it. OL depth Offensive line was another position Campbell pointed to that could make for tough decisions, but for opposite reasons than the defensive line. “Backend of the O-line is always going to be up (for grabs),” Campbell said. “I say that, there’s a chance that player’s not even here yet either.” In my opinion, the top eight players are likely somewhat set: Penei Sewell, Christian Mahogany, Juice Scruggs, Tate Ratledge, Blake Miller, Larry Borom, Ben Bartch, and Miles Frazier. A healthy debate could be made for Frazier, but I like his versatility and willingness to do anything the Lions asked of him this training camp. The question is whether anyone else on the roster warranted a spot on the 53-man roster. Many are likely to slot Seth McLaughlin in because Detroit has an obvious need for a backup center while Cade Mays is out, but I’m not entirely sure he’s earned his way onto the roster. Mason Miller made an incredible last push to make it by switching positions to center this week and playing well in the preseason finale despite no experience at the position. But I believe both of those players could clear waivers, make it to the practice squad, and be elevated early in the year for depth on game day. By only keeping eight, it allows Detroit the flexibility to keep a TE4 or WR6 or OL10 or DB11. And that’s why I chose that route. title: NFL waiver wire explained: Which Detroit Lions are impacted
summary: The NFL and the Detroit Lions will close out their preseason on Saturday, and by 6 p.m. ET Sunday, teams must reduce their rosters to 53 players. For the Lions, that will mean removing 38 players from their 91-man offseason roster, a daunting task that will need to be accomplished in roughly 24 hours after […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell, left, and general manager Brad Holmes walk off the field after practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The NFL and the Detroit Lions will close out their preseason on Saturday, and by 6 p.m. ET Sunday, teams must reduce their rosters to 53 players. For the Lions, that will mean removing 38 players from their 91-man offseason roster, a daunting task that will need to be accomplished in roughly 24 hours after they finish out the preseason. This look at the waiver wire process and how it impacts the Lions roster was sponsored by FanDuel Sportsbook , which currently has the Lions listed at +1700 to win this year’s Super Bowl, +850 to win the NFC Championship, and +155 to win the NFC North as the current favorites. Roster cuts: Waived vs. Released As Jeremy Reisman explained in a roster cuts rules article , when a player is cut from the roster, they’ll fall into two categories: “waived” or “released.” The category a player falls into depends on how many “credited” seasons in the NFL they have. A player earns a credited season if they spent at least three games in a season on the active roster, or the season on IR, or PUP . A player with four or more credited seasons is designated as “released,” meaning they immediately become a free agent. A player with fewer than four credited seasons is “waived” and therefore subject to the NFL’s waiver system, where another NFL team can claim them and keep their contract intact. Which Lions are eligible for the waiver wire? This offseason, the Lions got younger across the roster, and as a result, 57 of their 91 players have fewer than four credited seasons. Here’s a list of those players: (Projected starters are bolded ) QB Luke Altmyer RB Jahmyr Gibbs RB Sione Vaki RB Jacob Saylors RB Jabari Small RB Trayveon Williams RB Roydell Williams WR Isaac TeSlaa WR Tay Martin WR Dominic Lovett WR Malik Cunningham WR Lucky Jackson WR Tarik Black TE Sam LaPorta TE Jackson Meeks TE Thomas Gordon TE Zach Horton LG Christian Mahogany RG Tate Ratledge RT Blake Miller C Juice Scruggs OL Miles Frazier C Seth McLaughlin G Mason Miller OT Devin Cochran OT Giovanni Manu OL Melvin Priestly C/G Michael Niese OT Colby Sorsdal C Gus Hartwig DT Tyleik Williams DT Chris Smith DT Skyler Gill-Howard DT Mekhi Wingo DL Tyre West EDGE Tyler Lacy EDGE Derrick Moore EDGE Ahmed Hassanein EDGE Anthony Lucas EDGE Eric O’Neill LB Jimmy Rolder LB Trevor Nowaske LB Erick Hunter CB Ennis Rakestraw CB Nick Whiteside CB Keith Abney CB Ryan Cooper CB Ekow Boye-Doe CB Eric Scott DB Brian Branch DB Christian Izien S Thomas Harper DB Aamaris Brown S Dan Jackson S Jason Taylor II K Jake Bates LS Hogan Hatten Here’s an at-a-glance look at the Lions’ current depth chart, with the players eligible for the waiver wire colored by position and the vested veterans without color: Waiver wire priority From cutdowns through the first three weeks of the regular season, the waiver wire priority is determined by last year’s NFL Draft order, with teams in their original slots. That means the Lions will have 17th priority in the waiver wire process . Therefore, if they put in a claim for a “waived” player and the 16 teams ahead of them in the order do not put in a claim, Detroit will be awarded that player. Here’s the complete priority order: Las Vegas Raiders New York Jets Arizona Cardinals Tennessee Titans New York Giants Cleveland Browns Washington Commanders New Orleans Saints Kansas City Chiefs Cincinnati Bengals Miami Dolphins Dallas Cowboys Atlanta Falcons Baltimore Ravens Tampa Bay Buccaneers Indianapolis Colts Detroit Lions Minnesota Vikings Carolina Panthers Green Bay Packers Pittsburgh Steelers Los Angeles Chargers Philadelphia Eagles Jacksonville jaguars Chicago Bears Buffalo Bills Houston Texans San Francisco 49ers Los Angeles Rams Denver Broncos New England Patriots Seattle Seahawks Waiver wire timeframe Once a player is waived from any team, they become eligible for the waiver wire process, which begins immediately following cutdowns (Sunday at 6 p.m. ET) and ends on Monday at 1 p.m. ET. Once the deadline passes, the NFL will sort through the claims and award players based on waiver wire priority, with the highest priority getting first dibs. What happens after a player is claimed? Once a waived player is claimed by a team, that player is immediately placed on the team’s 53-man roster, and the team has until the end of the business day (typically only a few hours) to make a corresponding roster move. If the player cut to make room is eligible for the waiver wire, the process begins for them; they become eligible at 4 p.m. ET that day, and their waiver wire window closes the next day around noon. What happens if a player is not claimed? If a player is not claimed off waivers, they immediately become an unrestricted free agent and are eligible to sign with any team or to their practice squad. When do teams start building their practice squad? Once the initial waiver wire window expires (Monday at 1 p.m. ET), teams may begin building their 16-player practice squad—be on the lookout for our Practice Squad Tracker, which will publish on Sunday.

title: 6 Detroit Lions who improved their practice squad chances in preseason finale
summary: The preseason finale is not just about making a push for a roster spot. For many of these Detroit Lions players, it was their final audition to stay in the organization. The practice squad is as much a target as the initial 53-man roster for many players buried on the depth chart. Barring a massive […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 29: Lucky Jackson #11 of Detroit Lions celebrates after catching a pass against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The preseason finale is not just about making a push for a roster spot. For many of these Detroit Lions players, it was their final audition to stay in the organization. The practice squad is as much a target as the initial 53-man roster for many players buried on the depth chart. Barring a massive wave of injuries, some players simply have no path to the roster. Yet, securing a spot on the practice squad can be a way to build up experience and familiarity and, perhaps, become a contributor the following season. With the Lions toppling the Indianapolis Colts 25-16, they now enter the homestretch before roster cuts. Which players made enough of an impact to bolster their chances at the practice squad? Lucky Jackson, WR The wide receiver depth chart beyond Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa, and Greg Dortch has been wide open throughout training camp and preseason, yet there was no true breakout from anyone on the roster. While I think that Tay Martin is still the odds-on favorite to make the 53-man roster at this point, Jackson gave the Lions a lot to think about. He led the team with an impressive five catches for 94 yards, demonstrating some explosiveness and stellar hands. His only real negative was a miscommunication that led to Luke Altmyer’s interception. Despite the outstanding preseason finale, he remains a longshot to make the initial roster. The WR5 position is largely based on special teams, and Jackson does not excel either in coverage or as a returner, limiting his value. That being said, I think Jackson made a great case for the practice squad. None of Dominic Lovett, Tarik Black, Tom Kennedy, or Malik Cunningham have made this type of impact as a receiver. In the event of an injury on offense, he might be able to give the team some modest production. Amen Ogbongbemiga, LB Ogbongbemiga has been repping behind his linebacker competition (Trevor Nowaske, Joe Bachie, and Troy Reeder), but he has quietly been solid during preseason. For a smaller linebacker (6-foot-0 and 231 pounds), he has flashed both coverage ability and power as a blitzer. His calling card since joining the NFL has been special teams, and that has been no exception in Detroit—for a team that valued special teams ability from their depth players, Ogbongbemiga fits the bill. Given that Nowaske, Bachie, and Reeder have consistently seen the field before Ogbongbemiga, he remains on the outside looking in among the linebackers. That being said, his tape in preseason has shown enough to warrant practice squad consideration. Given that he can play nearly any linebacker position, that type of versatility makes him a valued veteran to keep around—and as a vested veteran, he would not be subject to waivers if cut. Eric O’Neill, DE Few players have impressed in preseason as much as O’Neill. On a weekly basis, he is making impact plays as a pass rusher, either bullying offensive linemen for a pressure or collapsing the pocket for his linemates to capitalize on. You could argue that he has been the most dominant pass rusher in preseason, even more so than Ahmed Hassanein. That being said, O’Neill still faces an uphill battle. O’Neill is more of a pass-rushing specialist at this point with limited value as a run stopper (he got bulldozed by a tight end on a Colts’ touchdown run). A hallmark of this Lions defense has been prioritizing run defense, and pass-rushing specialists have been few and far between on this roster—even when Al-Quaddin Muhammad was tearing it up as a pass rusher last season, his snaps were limited because he couldn’t defend the run. Coupled with a deep defensive line ahead of O’Neill and tight position battles throughout the roster, he seems destined for the practice squad. O’Neill remains a valuable project for the Lions to develop—assuming he clears waivers, of course. Trayveon Williams, RB Jacob Saylors dominated this game and could rise as high as RB2 by Week 1. However, he was not the only running back to impress against the Colts. Williams, signed only a few weeks ago, has quickly made a name for himself in preseason. He had a touchdown run last week against the Bengals and while he only garnered 36 yards on his 10 carries, it is worth noting that he was the Lions’ go-to short yardage option, thus lowering his average. His average was no concern on Saturday, finishing the game with 57 yards on nine carries. He also added a pair of touchdown rushes, also of the short yardage variety. He flashed some serious burst and power, burning the Colts defense on a few occasions (credit to a solid offensive line performance as well). There is likely no space for Williams on the 53-man roster, but he could be a valuable player to stash on the practice squad. Mason Miller, OL The bobbled snap is obviously a low point for Miller (a mistake that I criticized Michael Niese for in the first preseason game ), but that should not overshadow what was otherwise a phenomenal debut, of sorts. Miller had slotted in at guard for most of training camp and preseason, but with Cade Mays, Juice Scruggs, and Seth McLaughlin absent, Miller was the one to step into the literal center stage. Dan Campbell said he believes Mason Miller played "pretty dang clean" outside of one snap exchange mistake. Seth McLaughlin was in concussion protocol. — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) August 29, 2026 For someone with only a handful of days playing center as a professional, I thought Miller looked good. As a pass blocker, he was responsible for keeping Joshua Dobbs and Luke Altmyer clean for most of the game. As a run blocker, it was his bulldozing up the middle that helped spring Saylors and Williams on multiple rushes. Some of his snaps could use work, sure, but did anyone truly expect flawless snaps from a player with so little experience at the position? If anything, the fact that there weren’t more incidents is a testament to Miller’s outing. There was practically no chance for Miller to make the 53-man roster, but he made a good case to earn a place on the practice squad again in 2026—maybe not as a center, but at least he showed some adaptability. Aamaris Brown, S The Lions secondary depth chart is a logjam, so the chances of Brown winning a roster spot were slim from the start. All things considered, Brown showcased a lot to like as a developmental piece for 2026 and beyond. He has been a sound tackler throughout preseason and camp, with flashes in pass coverage. He had a pair of pass breakups against Indianapolis to go with his five tackles. He even added a pressure on one of his blitzing snaps, showcasing his ability to play deep or as a box safety. Brown was shaken up for a moment, so his injury status is worth monitoring. It is worth noting that with injuries to Brian Branch, Kerby Joseph, Christian Izien, Avonte Maddox, and Thomas Harper, the Lions’ safety group has been decimated. While that might not result in a roster spot for Brown, it could mean an early call-up if most of those names are not ready for Week 1.

title: Final 2026 Detroit Lions 53-man roster prediction: Jeremy Reisman edition
summary: As Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said following the team’s preseason finale, their win over the Indianapolis Colts provided some clarity at some positions and muddied the water at others. Both Campbell and general manager Brad Holmes will have some tough decisions ahead—and little time to make those roster choices. But I did my best […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 13: The Detroit Lions huddle up during the preseason game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images As Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said following the team’s preseason finale, their win over the Indianapolis Colts provided some clarity at some positions and muddied the water at others. Both Campbell and general manager Brad Holmes will have some tough decisions ahead—and little time to make those roster choices. But I did my best guess to predict those moves with my final 2026 Detroit Lions 53-man roster prediction. Side note: Don’t forget to check out Erik Schlitt’s 53-man prediction as well. Jeremy’s final Lions 53-man roster prediction Quarterback (2) Jared Goff Josh Dobbs Luke Altmyer Up until Saturday, I don’t think Dobbs had done anything to win the backup job, but that preseason finale was a nearly perfect performance. Meanwhile, while I think Altmyer was fine and a bit of a victim of circumstances, Saturday also highlighted his biggest weakness: processing speed. He held onto the ball too long, leading to a couple of sacks, including a lost fumble. I really like Altmyer’s potential, so I hope Detroit is able to keep him around on the practice squad and allow him to develop. Running back (4) Jahmyr Gibbs Isiah Pacheco Sione Vaki Jacob Saylors Jabari Small Trayveon Williams Roydell Williams This is relatively straightforward to me. The only question here is whether Isiah Pacheco’s injury will bleed into the regular season and if the Lions believe Vaki and Saylors would be adequate offensive help. Certainly, Saylor’s incredible play in the preseason finale will help ease some minds. Wide receiver (5) Amon-Ra St. Brown Jameson Williams Isaac TeSlaa Greg Dortch Tay Martin Dominic Lovett Tom Kennedy Malik Cunningham Lucky Jackson Tarik Black Season-ending IR: Kendrick Law There are only two questions here, in my opinion: who is WR5 and will the Lions consider a WR6? Tom Kennedy has a case for WR5, but his only contributions on special teams are as a returner, and Greg Dortch/Jacob Saylors should be able to handle those situations just as well. Tay Martin, on the other hand, has been repping at just about every special teams spot during training camp, and has made some flashes on offense, too. Kudos to Lucky Jackson for a phenomenal rebound after an early mental mistake on Saturday. It could be enough to make a difference, but Martin was also solid on Saturday and has been more consistent throughout camp. I opted not to keep a sixth out of necessity for more players elsewhere, including at…. Tight end (4) Sam LaPorta Brock Wright Tyler Conklin Jackson Meeks Thomas Gordon Zach Horton In my opinion, Meeks has shown enough growth to warrant consideration for keeping a fourth tight end. He’s also very capable on special teams. Here’s what Dan Campbell had to say after Meeks’ preseason game in Week 2. “He’s strong, and he’s willing, and he’s smart,” Campbell said. “So, it’s just time on task. He’s another one, but you see how he attacks special teams. He gives our guys fits on special teams, too.” Meeks struggled in blocking on Saturday, but his touchdown pass will only help his case. Offensive line (8) LT Penei Sewell LG Christian Mahogany C Juice Scruggs RG Tate Ratledge RT Blake Miller OT Larry Borom T/G Miles Frazier G Ben Bartch C Seth McLaughlin RG Mason Miller LT Devin Cochran LG Melvin Priestly RT Colby Sorsdal C/G Michael Niese C Gus Hartwig IR-to return: Cade Mays Reserve/Non-Football Injury: Giovanni Manu Mason Miller did just about all he could for me to seriously consider him for the eighth or ninth spot. What an incredible performance in the preseason finale as the emergency center with no experience. Ultimately, though, I’m not sure anyone earned that backup center job. So, instead, we’ll save a roster spot here, bring Miller or Seth McLaughlin—who is in concussion protocol—back via the practice squad, and elevate them as the backup for the first few weeks of the season. It’s unconventional and mildly risky, but I don’t think there’s a realistic shot Detroit loses either to waivers. Or maybe they find an upgrade at center elsewhere. I rostered Frazier because of his versatility and potential, and Bartch because he’s now healthy and I’m not counting out his chances to eventually truly challenge for a starting job, even with the season underway. Interior defensive line (5) 3T Alim McNeill DT Tyleik Williams 3T Skyler Gill-Howard DT Chris Smith DT Ben Stille 3T/5T Levi Onwuzurike 3T Mekhi Wingo DT Myles Adams 3T Tyre West In one of my final thoughts heading into the preseason, I claimed I’m not giving up on Levi Onwuzurike. But after a month of seeing him struggle with pad level and not make much of an impact, it’s hard for me to say he justified a spot on this roster. Saturday was the breaking point for me. He played into the second half and failed to make an impact, while the rest of the defensive line has been consistently making plays all August. Ben Stille also didn’t make any plays on Saturday, and he didn’t play until well after Onwuzurike, but he’s put together a better camp overall. And I can’t shake just how much Campbell gushed about Stille earlier this week, particularly his versatility to fill every spot—much like John Cominsky had in previous years. “What’s the intrigue with him is the versatility, man,” Campbell said of Stille. “He can play some big end, we think; he can play the nose certainly, and then three if you needed it. So the more you can do and the more that you can prove you can do, that is always going to help your case.” EDGE (5) EDGE Aidan Hutchinson EDGE DJ Wonnum Big End Tyler Lacy EDGE Derrick Moore Big End Ahmed Hassanein Rush End Anthony Lucas Rush End Eric O’Neill Nothing too surprising here. O’Neill has made a strong case late in camp and finished with a strong preseason game, but he’s likely to land on the practice squad if he clears waivers. He continues to notch pressures, but getting washed in the Colts’ touchdown run is something that I’m sure Campbell will remember. Linebacker (6) MIKE Jack Campbell SAM Derrick Barnes WILL Devin White WILL Malcolm Rodriguez SAM Trevor Nowaske MIKE Joe Bachie WILL Erick Hunter MIKE Troy Reeder WILL Amen Ogbongbemiga IR-to-return: Jimmy Rolder I made the tough decision to put Rolder on IR. While it seems like he’s nearly ready to return to practice, his lack of reps in training camp means he likely wouldn’t see the field much early in the season anyways. So let’s save the roster spot and get him back to practice in a month. No need to hurry it up. So where does his roster spot go? Bachie has been repping the highest of the bunch, has some defensive experience (seven starts), and is pretty dang good on special teams, too. That said, I would not be surprised if Reeder or Ogbongbemiga wins the job. Hunter is a fun project, but I don’t think the Lions have the roster space. Let’s hope he returns on the practice squad. Cornerback (7) CB D.J. Reed CB Rock Ya-Sin CB Nick Whiteside CB Ennis Rakestraw NB Keith Abney CB/NB Roger McCreary CB Khalil Dorsey CB Ryan “Bump” Cooper CB Ekow Boye-Doe CB Eric Scott This feels like a bit of overkill at cornerback, but Whiteside may be considered depth at safety at this point, and given the high injury rate at cornerback, I wouldn’t think twice about rostering seven. Rakestraw and McCreary are probably closest to the roster bubble, but Rakestraw brings untapped potential, and McCreary brings versatility as both an outside and inside guy. Neither player played particularly well in the finale, but at least Rakestraw finally got his big play with the interception. Safety (4) S Avonte Maddox S Chuck Clark NB/S Christian Izien S Thomas Harper DB Aamaris Brown S Dan Jackson DB Jason Taylor II Reserve/Physically Unable to Perform: Brian Branch, Kerby Joseph At this point, I think it’s a no-brainer to keep Branch…

title: 5 takeaways from the Lions’ preseason finale vs. Colts
summary: Saturday saw the preseason finale for the Detroit Lions take place at Lucas Oil Stadium against the Indianapolis Colts. The Lions would come away with the victory, 25-16, but the final score from an exhibition isn’t the main takeaway from this one. With so much at stake for the player’s competing for a spot on […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 29: Jacob Saylors #25 of Detroit Lions runs with the ball against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images Saturday saw the preseason finale for the Detroit Lions take place at Lucas Oil Stadium against the Indianapolis Colts. The Lions would come away with the victory, 25-16, but the final score from an exhibition isn’t the main takeaway from this one. With so much at stake for the player’s competing for a spot on the team’s 53-man roster, this was the last chance for those on the roster bubble to make an impression. Jacob Saylors leaves no doubt about his spot on the final roster After being one of the most productive running backs this preseason , Saylors has firmly stamped his spot on the 53-man roster. He had 14 touches across the 38 plays the Lions ran on offense in the first half—and two additional targets—which means he was the guy Detroit went to on nearly half of their plays to start the game. His 12 carries in the first half went for 67 yards, and his two catches resulted in 12 yards, but had Joshua Dobbs put a little more touch on a pass near the goal line, Saylors could have added a touchdown on his day. “Saylors is making a lot of runs,” Dan Campbell said during his halftime talk with Patti Cesarini. “All those guys have had some runs, but Saylors is taking advantage of that and he’s finding those creases.” Jabari Small suffered an injury on a kick return in the first quarter that required him to leave the game after spending time in the blue medical tent, so Saylors’ workday continued into the second half. Saylors’ strong play carried over into the second half where he continued to take advantage of the Colts’ depth defenders and the Lions push up front, finishing the game with 17 carries for 100 yards. Saylors with a pickup of 19 yards! Up to 100 yards on the day pic.twitter.com/cXkab0aobT — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 29, 2026 If the Lions are as shorthanded with injuries at the running back position as they are right now, Saylors could very well be in line to be a part of the offense in Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints. Luke Altmyer, Josh Dobbs make their final QB2 cases For the second game in a row, the first drive for the Lions offense resulted in another turnover. Luke Altmyer’s interception looked very similar to Dobbs’ mistake the previous week: rolling out to their right and throwing the ball back across the middle. The replay revealed that Lucky Jackson, who was blocking Sauce Gardner downfield and must have thought it was a run play, put him directly in the way of Thomas Gordon’s route—the intended receiver. To Altmyer’s credit, the UDFA bounced back on the very next series. He made some good throws, a balance of quick, decisive strikes to Greg Dortch and Tay Martin, as well as a pass to Lucky Jackson on third-and-9 for 19 yards that demonstrated Altmyer’s patience and feel. Leading a 10-play, 75-yard drive that ended with a 1-yard touchdown run by Trayveon Williams. The first play for the other quarterback vying for the backup job was nearly as disastrous when Mason Miller and Dobbs failed to cleanly exchange the ball under center. But much like Altmyer, Dobbs shook off the early misstep and outside of one missed throw to Saylors, the veteran arguably played even better than the UDFA. Dobbs was nearly perfect in the first half, completing 12 of 14 passes for 110 yards and two touchdowns. Meeeeeeeeeeeks pic.twitter.com/Bz4DsSHPDX — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 29, 2026 Altmyer’s second half resulted in another turnover when he held onto the ball too long, a problem that often plagues rookie quarterbacks. Campbell had made mention of wanting to see Altmyer make his way through progressions more confidently and concisely, and that will undoubtedly be a part of the young quarterback’s development, but have the Lions seen enough from Altmyer this summer to see his development through? Lucky Jackson shines as the WR5/6 battle comes down to the wire Lucky Jackson’s early gaffe that contributed to the Lions’ first turnover wasn’t going to define the receiver’s afternoon. Jackson immediately bounced back on the next drive, creating an explosive play for the Lions offense on third-and-9. Then, on Detroit’s final drive of the half, hauled in a one-handed catch for 35 yards, putting the Lions offense on the Colts’ 2-yard line. LUCKY. JACKSON. pic.twitter.com/h3ErfysAqs — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 29, 2026 Jackson was the leading receiver on the day, catching all five of his targets for 94 yards. Martin caught four passes for just 16 yards, but was on the receiving end of a touchdown pass from Dobbs, set up by that highlight-reel grab from Jackson. Dortch caught a couple of passes for 22 yards and nearly broke a punt return for a touchdown, and he’s set to be the team’s WR4. After Saturday’s game, it’s going to be a tough decision for Detroit when it comes to the WR5/6 spots. Skyler Gill-Howard puts exclamation point on impressive preseason If you haven’t heard about Skyler Gill-Howard yet, you must not be watching the games either because all he’s done this preseason is make one splashy play after another. Gill-Howard put the finishing touches on a very impressive summer by recording his first sack of the preseason, bringing down Anthony Richardson on third-and-5 to force a punt and end the Colts’ third drive of the afternoon. Sky LOCO 😤 pic.twitter.com/53huI3Foac — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 29, 2026 In addition to Gill-Howard, some other young players along Detroit’s defensive line made an impact on Saturday, including Eric O’Neill and Ahmed Hassanein. Both players recorded multiple pressures and each notched a quarterback hit on the day. Detroit’s depth along the defensive line will force the team to have some tough conversations before cutdowns tomorrow, but hopefully there’s an opportunity to keep some of these players developing with the team’s practice squad. Ennis Rakestraw caps roller-coaster preseason with a big play No Lions player has experienced the highs and lows of the summer quite like cornerback Ennis Rakestraw. After the way things ended in Week 1 against the Cincinnati Bengals, you would have wondered if Rakestraw was going to be healthy enough to compete for a spot on the final roster. But after stringing together some strong play in practice, and a better performance against the Washington Commanders in Week 2, Rakestraw had this final game to make his case. Hassanein + O'Neill pressure = a Rakestraw Jr. INT! pic.twitter.com/qHpgR1fZ2g — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 29, 2026 It wasn’t all perfect for Rakestraw against the Colts on Saturday. He got picked on a couple of times during the Colts’ fourth drive on offense, allowing a 25-yard completion on fourth-and-6 and a 14-yard completion on the very next play to set up the only touchdown for Indianapolis on the day. But after Trayveon Williams fumbled the ensuing kick return, Rakestraw jumped a route on third-and-10 and picked off a pass from Riley Leonard to keep the Colts off the board and flip the field back in Detroit’s favor. With all of the uncertainty in Detroit’s secondary due to injury—Nick Whiteside almost exclusively played safety Saturday—things have certainly turned in Rakestraw’s favor since the start of training camp.

title: Detroit Lions final 53-man roster prediction: Erik Schlitt edition
summary: With the Detroit Lions’ final preseason game on the books, the front office and coaching staff are now tasked with reducing their 91-man roster down to 53 players by 6 p.m. ET on Sunday, a challenging task to complete over the next 24 hours. As is tradition, Jeremy Reisman and I will each publish our own projections […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 08: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions looks on and smiles before the game against the Carolina Panthers at Ford Field on October 08, 2023 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the Detroit Lions’ final preseason game on the books, the front office and coaching staff are now tasked with reducing their 91-man roster down to 53 players by 6 p.m. ET on Sunday, a challenging task to complete over the next 24 hours. As is tradition, Jeremy Reisman and I will each publish our own projections of what we think the Lions 53-man roster could look like, so make sure you check his out as well . But without further ado, here is how I see things playing out. Erik’s final Lions 53-man roster prediction Quarterback (2) Jared Goff Josh Dobbs Luke Altmyer The QB2 battle was tight until the very end, with both quarterbacks leading the offense to at least one touchdown in the first half of the preseason finale. While I love Altmyer’s upside, I’m not quite sure he’s ready to take on the QB2 role. And when you add in that Lions coaches tend to prefer a veteran in the QB2 role, and with Dobbs showing well in the finale, I’m picking him for the role. Running back (4) Jahmyr Gibbs Isiah Pacheco Sione Vaki Jacob Saylors Trayveon Williams Jabari Small Roydell Williams The big question for me here is Pacheco’s health. If he ends up on injured reserve, then that opens the door for Trayveon Williams, who had a very strong camp challenging for the RB4 role, but Saylors was simply too consistent and earned the role with his versatility on offense and special teams. Wide receiver (5) Amon-Ra St. Brown Jameson Williams Isaac TeSlaa Greg Dortch Tay Martin Tom Kennedy Lucky Jackson Dominic Lovett Malik Cunningham Tarik Black Season-ending IR: Kendrick Law The battle for WR5 came down to Martin vs. Kennedy for me, and I felt like Martin just did a little bit more on offense and special teams, giving him the edge. I also debated keeping a WR6 but ended up sticking with what they’ve done in recent history and used this roster spot elsewhere on defense. Lucky Jackson surely made things interesting in the preseason finale, and he’s had a consistent, slow climb up the depth chart throughout camp, making him a potential “surprise” player who could make the team. At a minimum, he should be a practice squader. Tight end (3) Sam LaPorta Brock Wright Tyler Conklin Jackson Meeks Thomas Gordon Zach Horton One of my final decisions was whether to keep a fourth tight end—which would have been Jackson Meeks—but I ultimately went with a ninth offensive lineman instead. Meeks has been terrific on offense and special teams through camp and the preseason games, but I think he’ll sneak through waivers, make the practice squad, and could be a game-day elevation early in the season—which could result in his eventual path to the active roster. Offensive line (9 + 2 injured) LT Penei Sewell LG Christian Mahogany C Juice Scruggs RG Tate Ratledge RT Blake Miller OT Larry Borom T/G Miles Frazier G Ben Bartch C Seth McLaughlin RG Mason Miller LT Devin Cochran LG Melvin Priestly RT Colby Sorsdal C/G Michael Niese C Gus Hartwig IR/Eligible to return : C Cade Mays NFI : OT Giovanni Manu With Cade Mays likely moving to injured reserve to start the season, the starters are locked in. Borom and Frazier are also easy additions, while Bartch and McLaughlin (OL8 and OL9) have done enough to warrant a spot, but still need to prove themselves. McLaughlin’s injury worries me because of the unknown, but I think he gives the Lions the best option as a temporary reserve center. The main concern with Bartch is durability, but he is a steady veteran who provides great depth. Interior defensive line (5) 3T Alim McNeill DT Tyleik Williams 3T/5T Levi Onwuzurike 3T Skyler Gill-Howard DT Chris Smith 3T Mekhi Wingo DT Ben Stille DT Myles Adams 3T Tyre West After preseason Game 2, I had a hard time separating Smith, Wingo, and Stille in the DT5 competition, but Smith’s consistency throughout camp and his performance in the finale (starting and repping ahead of his competitors) won me over. Wingo is a tough cut for me because the Lions utilize him in a lot of ways, but his game is similar to Gill-Howard, and I think the rookie locked up a spot with his play this offseason. EDGE (5) EDGE Aidan Hutchinson EDGE DJ Wonnum Big End Tyler Lacy EDGE Derrick Moore Big End Ahmed Hassanein Rush End Anthony Lucas Rush End Eric O’Neill The Lions like to deploy two different styles of defensive end opposite Hutchinson, with Wonnum and Lacy filling out those starting roles. Moore and Hassanein locked up reserve rotational roles at each spot early in camp, leaving a difficult path for the UDFA rookies. Both Lucas and O’Neill should be candidates for the practice squad. Linebacker (6) MIKE Jack Campbell SAM Derrick Barnes WILL Devin White WILL Malcolm Rodriguez MIKE Jimmy Rolder SAM Trevor Nowaske MIKE Joe Bachie MIKE Troy Reeder WILL Amen Ogbongbeniga WILL Erick Hunter From a talent perspective, I’m very comfortable with the top six. But with Rolder still not practicing and Nowaske suffering a late-camp injury, this group was a bit harder to predict than originally anticipated. If Rolder isn’t ready to play in Week 1, adding a player like Bachie to the practice squad and elevating him for the first game makes sense. Then again, if Rolder ends up on injured reserve, it could open the door for Bachie to make the roster outright. Cornerback (7) CB D.J. Reed CB Rock Ya-Sin NB Keith Abney CB Nick Whiteside CB Ennis Rakestraw CB Khalil Dorsey CB/NB Roger McCreary CB Ryan “Bump” Cooper CB Ekow Boye-Doe CB Eric Scott If the Lions end up needing another spot on offense (i.e they want a TE4 and OL9), this group could probably withstand the loss of some depth. Reed and Ya-Sin are locked in on the outside, and Abney is being used inside in some starting packages. Whiteside has been steady throughout camp and is getting cross-trained at safety for depth, while Rakestraw may have erased some concerns with that interception in the preseason finale. Dorsey is far too valuable on special teams, leaving the versatile McCreary as the possible last man in and most vulnerable. Safety (4 + 2 injured) S Avonte Maddox S Chuck Clark NB/S Christian Izien S Thomas Harper DB Aamaris Brown S Dan Jackson DB Jason Taylor II PUP : S Brian Branch, Kerby Joseph I am projecting Branch and Joseph to start the season on PUP, leaving Maddox and Clark as the starters, as they’ve been throughout camp. Izien will start at nickel—splitting time with Abney—and Harper should give them enough depth to feel comfortable… assuming everyone is healthy. Health is the big issue with this group, as Maddox, Izien, Harper, Brown, and Jackson all ended camp with an injury. At this time, it doesn’t appear any are dealing with something long-term that would warrant a stint on injured reserve, but there could be some shake-ups here if certain injuries linger. title: Green Bay Packers will have 2nd shot at running back Damon Bankston
summary: If you’re an avid reader of Acme Packing Company, you know that I feel like the Green Bay Packers show their cards a bit when it comes to pre-draft visitors. Since 2022, when the Packers appeared to have changed their visit strategy from almost being used exclusively on undrafted free agent rookie recruiting to more […]
full_text: PHOENIX, AZ - DECEMBER 26: New Mexico Lobos running back Damon Bankston (1) runs back a kickoff for a touchdown during the Rate Bowl college football game between the New Mexico Lobos and the Minnesota Golden Gophers on December 26, 2025 at Chase Field in Phoenix, Arizona. (Photo by Kevin Abele/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If you’re an avid reader of Acme Packing Company, you know that I feel like the Green Bay Packers show their cards a bit when it comes to pre-draft visitors . Since 2022, when the Packers appeared to have changed their visit strategy from almost being used exclusively on undrafted free agent rookie recruiting to more of a mix of picks and free agent prospects, Green Bay has signed, traded for, drafted or claimed on waivers 36 players who were pre-draft visitors with the team. Often, when these players become available (some of them never become available, because they were high draft picks who were picked before the Packers were on the clock), Green Bay ends up targeting them in some way or another. While players like Darian Kinnard, John FitzPatrick and Josh Whyle weren’t originally picked by the Packers, they did find their way to Green Bay later in their careers. So, when a pre-draft visitor becomes available, my radar always goes up, especially if it’s the first time the Packers have had a shot at bringing them to Green Bay since draft weekend. That’s the case right now with New York Giants running back Damon Bankston, who was waived by the team on Saturday . Bankston took a pre-draft visit with the Packers this spring, but ended up signing with the Giants for $115,000 guaranteed, far more than Green Bay spent on their UDFA running back signing, Jaden Nixon — who was added to the offseason roster for $15,000 guaranteed . The New Mexico product was an interesting sleeper prospect in the class of 2026, as he posted 635 rushing yards (5.6 yards per carry), five touchdowns on the ground and caught 31 balls for 397 yards and three touchdowns (12.8 yards per reception, a very high number for backs) through the air in his one year of FBS football. The numbers don’t exactly look incredible from a volume perspective, but he was very efficient in the 9-4 Lobos’ running back by committee (and he led the team in yards from scrimmage). Before his stint at New Mexico, Bankston was an All-Conference player and team captain at Weber State, an FCS program. He also saw time as a returner at the college level. If the Packers’ preseason film is any indication (and I’m not sure I’m sold on the idea), Green Bay’s offense is going to look a lot more like the early Matt LaFleur years in 2026, with more outside zone runs and bootlegs off of outside zone action . To run those plays, you need some home run hitters in the backfield, like Aaron Jones was for LaFleur when he got the offense going in Green Bay. While he’s not the biggest back at 5’10” and 196 pounds, Bankston does have 4.43-second 40-yard dash speed and also put up an elite 6.89-second three-cone during his pre-draft process. Damon Bankston is a RB prospect in the 2026 draft class. He scored a 8.13 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 425 out of 2268 RB from 1987 to 2026. https://t.co/YsK1v58Obp pic.twitter.com/6JChHWvpTv — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 2, 2026 For whatever reason, things didn’t work for Bankston in New York, as the Giants continued to add players at the position this offseason, including Najee Harris, who has been linked to the Harbaugh family since then-Michigan head coach Jim Harbaugh was hosting satellite recruiting camps at his high school campus . If the Packers didn’t feel like committing to Bankston’s requested guarantees back in April, here’s some good news: There’s no dibs on practice squad players. We’ve seen Green Bay poach a couple of these guys, not via waivers, but by being a players’ preferred practice squad location, every year. Generally, when those players have been pre-draft visitors, like tight end Josh Whyle was last year after he was waived by the Tennessee Titans, they tend to get onto the regular season field quicker than a typical practice squadder. Just keep an eye out for Bankston, and don’t be surprised if he’s an addition on Monday — or a future date, if the Packers feel like their running back room is fine going into Week 1. It’s not like Bankston exactly lit up the preseason, as he recorded 21 rushing attempts for 73 yards (3.5 YPC) and had two receptions for two yards, but Green Bay was interested in him at one point, and he’s a pretty good system fit for what the Packers’ offense has been putting up on film. Beggars can’t be choosers, either. Those 73 yards on the ground would have led all of the Packers’ backs this preseason.

title: Packers Roster Cut Tracker 2026
summary: Sunday, August 30th is a big day for the NFL this year. In 2026, the league has set the deadline for teams to cut their rosters down from 90 players to 53 for Sunday at 6:00 PM Eastern Time (5:00 Central), an odd time compared to recent deadlines. Recent years have seen the league require […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - AUGUST 02: Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFluer and General Manager Brian Gutekunst look on during the annual Green Bay Packers Family night practice at Lambeau Field on August 2nd, 2025 in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Sunday, August 30th is a big day for the NFL this year. In 2026, the league has set the deadline for teams to cut their rosters down from 90 players to 53 for Sunday at 6:00 PM Eastern Time (5:00 Central), an odd time compared to recent deadlines. Recent years have seen the league require cuts come in on the Tuesday following the final week of preseason games, giving front offices a few extra days. This year, however, the league’s decision to hold a game in Australia in week one led it to push the cutdown date a bit earlier. Green Bay Packers general manager Brian Gutekunst revealed that in a press conference earlier this week, noting that while not a fan of the shift, there’s not really anything he or the other 31 GMs around the league can do about it. That means that the Packers will have a little less than 48 hours from the completion of their final preseason game (around 10 PM Central on Friday night) to the cut-down deadline. Here at Acme Packing Company, we will be following along with all of the Packers’ moves to get from 90 to 53, which will include releases, players going on the reserve/PUP list, and more. The Reserve/Physically Unable to Perform list is one mechanism for teams to keep players on their roster in a reserve role if they failed a physical exam before training camp, went on the active/PUP list to start camp, and stayed there all summer long. Players who go on reserve/PUP to start the regular season do not count against the 53-man limit, but they may not be activated until after their team’s fourth regular season game, though they can start practicing after two games have passed. The Packers have four players still on the active/PUP who are eligible for the reserve/PUP to start the season: Luke Musgrave, Matt Orzech, Micah Parsons, and Jordon Riley. Parsons has generally been targeting the Packers’ week 6 game against his old team, the Dallas Cowboys, for his return. Perhaps surprisingly, he is not seen as one of the favorites to win the NFL’s Comeback Player of the Year award; FanDuel sportsbook has his odds at just +3500 , good for 10th in the NFL. That slots in behind teammate Tucker Kraft (7th, +2700), while a host of quarterbacks like Patrick Mahomes, Kyler Murray, and Jayden Daniels lead the way. title: NFL Waiver Rules & Order: Packers sit 20th at cutdown deadline
summary: The NFL’s roster cut deadline is fast approaching, and with it comes one of the more convoluted and hectic days of the league’s schedule. Sunday’s cut-down leads to chaos the following day, when players subject to waivers can either be claimed by new teams or become free agents. At that time, teams will also begin […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - AUGUST 23: Green Bay Packers General Manager Brian Gutekunst looks on prior to a preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and the Seattle Seahawks on August 23, 2025 at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The NFL’s roster cut deadline is fast approaching, and with it comes one of the more convoluted and hectic days of the league’s schedule. Sunday’s cut-down leads to chaos the following day, when players subject to waivers can either be claimed by new teams or become free agents. At that time, teams will also begin assembling practice squads, making it an especially crazy day around the league. The Green Bay Packers could be active on waivers, perhaps looking to add to the running back or tight end position from the list of players released around the league. Ahead of that process getting started, let’s get a quick refresher on how all of this works. Waiver Rules & Timing NFL teams must reduce their rosters from 90 players to 53 by 6:00 PM Eastern (5:00 PM Central) on Sunday, August 30th. At that time, players who are released go into one of two statuses based on their level of accrued experience in the NFL. Players with four or more accrued seasons of experience are defined as vested veterans and, when released, immediately become free agents who are eligible to sign with any team in the NFL. Those with three or fewer accrued seasons, however, are subject to waivers. Teams hoping to sign a player on waivers must submit a waiver claim, and the player’s rights are awarded to whichever team has the highest waiver priority among the teams submitting claims. Normally, a waived player will have their waiver process cleared one day after their release is formally processed, taking place at the end of the league’ official day (4:00 PM Eastern). However, the waiver process for players released during final cuts will clear instead at 12:00 Noon Eastern on Monday, August 31st. After that time, any players who do not receive a claim become free agents and are eligible to sign with any team. Teams may also begin signing these free agent players to their practice squads after the waiver claim deadline. Current Waiver Order At final cuts, the NFL orders waivers in reverse order of the previous year’s final standings, mirroring the order from the first round of the NFL Draft (before any trades were processed). The Green Bay Packers would have selected 20th had they not traded their first-round pick away in the Micah Parsons deal, so that is their position in waivers when they process after cuts. Here’s the full order: Las Vegas Raiders New York Jets Arizona Cardinals Tennessee Titans New York Giants Cleveland Browns Washington Commanders New Orleans Saints Kansas City Chiefs Cincinnati Bengals Miami Dolphins Dallas Cowboys Atlanta Falcons Baltimore Ravens Tampa Bay Buccaneers Indianapolis Colts Detroit Lions Minnesota Vikings Carolina Panthers Green Bay Packers Pittsburgh Steelers Los Angeles Chargers Philadelphia Eagles Jacksonville Jaguars Chicago Bears Buffalo Bills San Francisco 49ers Houston Texans Los Angeles Rams Denver Broncos New England Patriots Seattle Seahawks Of course, the Packers are 20th on this list because they had the second-worst record of the teams who lost in the first round of the playoffs last season (ahead of only the Panthers). Green Bay would love to be 32nd on this list next season, but that would require a Super Bowl win. According to FanDuel sportsbook , the Packers’ Super Bowl odds are currently +2200, putting them in a tie for 13th with a few other teams across the NFL.

title: Packers wide receivers make their cases in final preseason game
summary: Earlier in the preseason I suggested the Packers open up their wide receiver competition. I don’t know if the Packers’ brass got the message, but the receivers on the lower end of the roster certainly lived up to their end of the bargain. The third preseason game was a 60 minute wide receiver showcase, with […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - AUGUST 28: Green Bay Packers wide receiver Kisean Johnson (86) scores the game winning touchdown during a preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and the Arizona Cardinals on August 28, 2026 at Lambeau Field, in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Earlier in the preseason I suggested the Packers open up their wide receiver competition . I don’t know if the Packers’ brass got the message, but the receivers on the lower end of the roster certainly lived up to their end of the bargain. The third preseason game was a 60 minute wide receiver showcase, with several contenders putting up their best statistical performances of the exhibition slate. J. Michael Sturdivant has been perhaps the strongest contender and put together the best statistical performance of any Packers receiver this preseason so far. He caught six passes for 112 yards and a touchdown, the score coming on a beautifully designed play that sprung him down the left sideline for six. Sturdivant finishes the preseason with nine catches for 142 yards and a touchdown. Just as importantly, he played 19 snaps on special teams during the Packers’ three preseason games, including six and three, respectively, on the Packers’ crucial punt and kickoff coverage units. I don’t know if it’s enough to make the 53 man roster, but that’s about all you could ask for from an undrafted player trying to make a case for himself. Isaiah Neyor has been the next strongest roster contender, and his stats have been more steady than spectacular. He had ten total catches across three preseason games, finishing with exactly 100 yards. He failed to find the end zone, but that doesn’t mean much in preseason competition, when opportunities can be inconsistent and quarterback play can be spotty. Neyor actually played a bit more on special teams than Sturdivant, logging 21 snaps in three games, but 10 of those snaps came on kickoff return, which is a lower priority than the coverage units. Will Sheppard was the next most productive receiver. Due to being a bit smaller (but not much) than both Sturdivant and Neyor, I think most roster watchers have penciled him in behind his bigger-bodied counterparts, but he showed up against the Cardinals in a big way. He caught three passes for 26 yards and a score, but his real highlight was an 81-yard punt return for his second touchdown of the evening. If big plays carry weight in roster competitions, no wide receiver made a bigger one than that. Sheppard finished the preseason with 10 catches for 81 yards and two touchdowns. Finally, Kisean Johnson saved his best for last. Signed by the Packers on August 9, Johnson has come along slowly and his opportunities have been more limited than the rest of the lower-end receivers, but he made up some ground (statistically, at least) on Friday night. Johnson caught four passes for 52 yards and two touchdowns, including the game-winner to cap off the Packers’ two-minute drive to end the game. Those catches represented his full statistical output in this year’s preseason, but it was an eye-catching performance, to be sure. As impressive as each of these players may have been, the harsh reality is they’re competing for maybe one roster spot. Christian Watson, Jayden Reed, and Matthew Golden have roster spots locked up, as does Savion Williams (despite injuries and generally unimpressive play). Beyond those four, Bo Melton and Skyy Moore seem like good bets as special teams contributors. For any of the four receivers we talked about in this piece to have a shot, the Packers would have to keep seven wide receivers on their initial 53-man roster. That’s not unheard of, but it shows how tenuous the life of a player on the roster bubble can be: no matter how well you perform, the ruthless accounting of NFL roster building still might mean you end up out of a job.
