title: 2026 NFL offseason trade grades: Gervon Dexter, Broderick Jones
summary: We're making sense of seven big preseason deals, including Broderick Jones to the Cowboys.
full_text:
The main transaction window of the 2026 NFL offseason is over, with free agency and the draft long behind us. But teams are still leaning on trades to improve their rosters between now and Week 1. And we're grading the biggest swaps around the league, putting each deal into perspective for teams.

 The post-June 1 deals started with a bang. The Browns are  trading  edge rusher  Myles Garrett to the Rams for multiple draft picks -- including a 2027 first-rounder -- and edge rusher Jared Verse . The Patriots finally made their move to bring in Eagles wide receiver  A.J. Brown , giving up two draft picks. Did the Rams overpay in a massive return for Cleveland? Does Brown complete New England's offense? How do we feel about the Falcons acquiring offensive tackle Wanya Morris , the Texans getting wide receiver  Kayshon Boutte  and the Rams bringing back  wide receiver  Tutu Atwell ? And how did trades ahead of cut-down day impact the Cowboys, Steelers, Bears and Falcons?

 To determine each grade, we are looking at multiple factors, including on-field impact, salary cap implications, compensation, player value/age and the context of a team's short- and long-term outlooks. How large is the effect of this decision, and how sure are we that it's a good or bad choice? How does this affect a team's chance to win the Super Bowl, this season or in the future?

 Let's get into our grades, and check back throughout training camp and the preseason for more trade evaluations.

 
 See more: 
 Tracking trades over the summer 
 Grades from earlier in the offseason 

 
 

 

 Bears trade DT Dexter to Falcons 
 Falcons get: DT  Gervon Dexter Sr . 
 Bears get: CB Clark Phillips III , fifth-round pick

 Falcons grade : A- 
 Bears grade : C

 This a good get for the Falcons, who needed defensive tackle help worse than perhaps any other team in the league. Free agent addition Da'Shawn Hand has missed most of training camp with a leg injury, leaving only bottom-of-the-roster contributors to fill the starting spot besides Brandon Dorlus . In Dexter, the Falcons grab a player big enough to play the nose next to Dorlus, but with enough power and pass-rush technique to still matter on passing downs.

 Dexter had a pressure rate of 10.5% last season by NFL Next Gen Stat's charting, 11th among all defensive tackles and well above the league average for defensive tackles (7.4%). It is worth remarking that Dexter isn't really a penetrator who creates his own pressure -- he only had 4 quick pressures on the season, and his 1.13 second get-off was among the slowest of defensive tackles last season. Dexter is a pocket-pusher who needs other pass rushers to create the first disruption. On a line that features Dorlus and second-year pro James Pearce Jr . (when he returns from his eight-game suspension ), that role can make sense.

 Dexter is on a contract year, which is one of the reasons he was available for a cheap return. If he has a good year in Atlanta, the Falcons might consider extending him... but they might also let him walk for a compensatory pick that replaces (or improves upon) the fifth-rounder they lost in letting him go.

 The Bears have waited on a leap forward in consistency from Dexter over the past two seasons, and absent a real breakout, have moved on to a rotation of veteran free agents ( Neville Gallimore , Kentavius Street and James Lynch ) and the exciting preseason play of rookie sixth-round pick Jordan van den Berg . All of those players, along with incumbent Grady Jarrett , are better suited to playing 3-tech than they are the nose. It's worth wondering if the Bears have a second incoming move to beef up their position at the nose.

 The Bears add CB Clark Phillips III , a depth player who has largely played outside in his career (727 snaps) but has the size to perhaps excel in the slot instead -- he only has 37 career snaps on the inside. The Bears anticipate playing fourth-round rookie Malik Muhammad in the slot as Kyler Gordon returns from injury, but depth at outside corner is also important given Jaylon Johnson 's injury background and Tyrique Stevenson 's history of uneven play. Phillips is nice for depth, but not much of a needle mover when a starter is going back the other way. -- Ben Solak 

 

 

 Steelers trade OT Jones to Cowboys 
 Cowboys get:  OT Broderick Jones , 2027 fourth-round pick 
 Steelers get: 2027 third- and sixth-round picks

 Cowboys grade: B- 
 Steelers grade: B

 This time last year, Broderick Jones was the starting left tackle for the Pittsburgh Steelers -- in line to replace the outgoing Dan Moore Jr . Hopes were high after Jones was drafted in 2023 out of Georgia, where he developed skills at right tackle in his last two seasons.

 But Jones struggled mightily when moved to left tackle with the Steelers. His pass block win rate on true pass sets last season was 65th of 68 qualifying tackles across the first 11 weeks of the 2025 season. A Week 12 neck injury then shelved Jones for the rest of the season . ESPN's Adam Schefter reported in April that Jones suffered setbacks during his recovery and his availability for offseason activities and Week 1 was uncertain. Those health concerns, along with his poor 2025 play, contributed to the Steelers' selection of Arizona State's Max Iheanachor in the first round of the 2026 draft. Jones did return to the field at the start of training camp, but the writing was on the wall for the lineman, who was still playing into the fourth quarter of Thursday's preseason game.

 The Steelers got a solid return for a player they could have feasibly cut on Sunday -- that's always good business on cut-down day. Though, it is a little scary to walk into Week 1 with poor tackle depth behind Iheanachor and left tackle Troy Fautanu , both of whom have injury histories.

 The Cowboys take a big swing on a talented athlete at a position in which they have had some instability, and returning Jones to the right could help him return to his previous form of play. The Cowboys have yet to confirm which side is the plan for Jones, as left tackle Tyler Guyton started the year in a camp competition but reportedly impressed with a great summer, while right tackle Terence Steele -- a long-time starter under contract through 2028 -- hasn't had the best play in past seasons. Ostensibly, Jones is better on the right and has a better path to reps on the right ... but the recent film and injury history is scary to buy into, no matter the side. -- Solak 

 

 

 Dolphins trade WR Atwell to Rams 
 Date: Aug. 27 

 Rams get: WR Tutu Atwell 
 Dolphins get: RB Jarquez Hunter 

 Rams grade: B 
 Dolphins grade: B

 It's safe to say that no team likes Atwell as much as the Rams. A year ago, the Rams re-signed him to a one-year, $10 million deal that raised eyebrows at the time (and still does now). Atwell was coming off a season in which he recorded 562 receiving yards but had done so on 2.2 yards per route run. But the $10 million wasn't worth it -- he ran a route on just 35% of Rams dropbacks last season and amassed only 192 receiving yards (1.4 yards per route run).

 

 The Rams let him walk in free agency, with the Dolphins signing him to a one-year, $1.4 million contract . But apparently Atwell could not hang in Miami, even against a weak receiving group that included Malik Washington , Jalen Tolbert and several rookies, such as third-rounders Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell .

 The fact the Rams are bringing him back is telling about how they feel about their receiver depth. After Puka Nacua and Davante Adams , the depth chart is awfully lackluster, with Jordan Whittington , Konata Mumpfield , Xavier Smith and rookie  CJ Daniels . The Rams play a lot of tight ends -- they played 13 personnel (one RB, three TEs) more than twice as much any other team last season -- but there will still be snaps when they need three wide receivers on the field. And there's no guarantee Nacua and Adams are available all season.

title: 2026 NFL projected sack leaders: Top 50 pass rushers
summary: Will Aidan Hutchinson topple Myles Garrett as the sack champion? What about Micah Parsons? Seth Walder projects this season's top sack-getters.
full_text:
Myles Garrett broke the single-season sack record last season, but a different edge rusher leads our 2026 sack projections.

 That player? The Detroit Lions ' Aidan Hutchinson , who our statistical model forecasts to rack up 12.5 sacks this season.

 This is the sixth consecutive year we've run our sack forecast for veteran pass rushers based on a statistical model that uses information about a player's past performance and current circumstances to project how many sacks he will record in the upcoming season. The model's inputs include:

 
 Sack totals and rates for each of the past two seasons 
 Projected snaps, via ESPN's Mike Clay 
 Pass rush win rate, which uses data from NFL Next Gen Stats 
 Past sack rates for the quarterbacks on each player's schedule 
 Team win totals from the betting market 
 Where a player aligns 
 Age 
 
Only defensive linemen and edge rushers are included, and rookies are excluded. Also, though we recently upgraded our pass rush win rate metrics , this analysis features the legacy version of that metric. Future years will incorporate the upgrades. These projections often appear low. However, they are a projection of a player's mean outcome in 2026 -- including injuries. If we could guarantee health for every player, everyone's forecast would be much higher.
 Now, let's dive into the 2026 projections, looking at the top 10 forecasts, plus a few other notables (including one outside the top 50). There's also a top-50 list below. 

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Projected top 10 | Full top-50 list 
 More notable projections to watch 

 
 

 

 1. Aidan Hutchinson , Detroit Lions 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 12.5 
 2025 sack total: 14.5

 This is the second straight year that Hutchinson leads our sack projections, despite having never actually led the league in sacks. But everything lines up for him to have a huge season.

 Two years ago, he had a prolific first five games (7.5 sacks, 35% pass rush win rate) before suffering a season-ending leg injury . Last season, Hutchinson stayed healthy and delivered 14.5 sacks in 17 games. If anything, this projection might be underrating Hutchinson, because while his legacy pass rush win rate was above average, he moved up to fourth among edge rushers in the updated version.

 The other big reason Hutchinson's forecast is so strong is playing time. Unlike many pass rushers, Hutchinson rarely comes off the field. He played 91% of his possible defensive snaps last season, a much higher rate than players such as Will Anderson Jr . (66%) or Nik Bonitto (62%).

 Hutchinson has two other perks working in his favor, the quality of the Lions' overall team (eighth in ESPN's Football Power Index ) and the ease of their schedule (second easiest, according to FPI). That means Detroit should be ahead often, which is when sacks most frequently occur.

 
 

 

 2. Micah Parsons , Green Bay Packers 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 11.1 
 2025 sack total: 12.5

 The X factor is how much Parsons will play. Clay has Parsons projected to play 619 snaps this season, slightly down from the 669 he played in 14 games in 2025 -- which indicates a slight increase in snaps per game if Parsons were to come back from his knee injury in Week 6 and play the rest of the season. Still, it's incredible that Parsons is projected to miss a third of the season yet still manages to have the second-best forecast.

 How?

 If we compare him to Myles Garrett , Parsons had a better pass rush win rate in each of the past two seasons, more sacks per game two years ago, is more than three years younger and is on a team that blitzes more. But if there's one overriding reason Parsons is ranked here, it's the combination of win rates alongside his previous double-digit sack seasons.

 Parsons is a master of winning on a down-to-down basis but has never had more than 14 sacks in a season. But that could happen at any moment.

 

 

 3. Will Anderson Jr ., Houston Texans 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.5 
 2025 sack total: 12

 Anderson emerged as truly elite in 2025, finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting to go along with his 12 sacks. There's no reason to expect a drop-off this season.

 Anderson has proved himself the past two seasons in terms of sacks and pass rush win rate, is young and on a relatively good team (the Texans' win total at DraftKings is 9.5 , shaded to the over) with a particularly good defense. He and Danielle Hunter (8.7 projected sacks, 12th most) make up arguably the NFL's most fearsome pass rushing duo.

 Plus, the Texans get the additional bonus of facing a sack-friendly schedule of quarterbacks that includes games against Lamar Jackson (9.8% sack rate), Justin Herbert (8.8%), Jaxson Dart (8.5%) and Cam Ward (9.4%) twice.

 

 

 4. Nik Bonitto , Denver Broncos 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.3 
 2025 sack total: 14

 Bonitto backed up his breakout 13.5-sack campaign in 2024 with 14 sacks in 2025. This season, he gets the benefit of being part of a Broncos defense that is not only strong overall (with great cornerbacks) but also blitzes at an above-average rate.

 If there's one thing holding Bonitto back, it's playing time. Last season, he only played 62% of Denver's defensive snaps and was in only 60% of the time in clear pass-rushing situations. That puts a ceiling on his forecast. In addition, Bonitto is a player we might be overrating based on the use of the legacy win rates, which were higher on him than the updated version released a week ago. Still, this is a mighty strong projection.

 

 

 5. Myles Garrett , Los Angeles Rams 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.1 
 2025 sack total: 23

 Yes, I'm as surprised as you are that Garrett is not No. 1 on this list. Even though I know how the model works, I still thought the NFL-record 23 sacks from last season would be enough to put him over the top. Not quite, it turns out!

 There are three primary factors working against Garrett:

 
 1. He is 30 years old 
 2. The Rams blitzed only 19% of the time last season, the second-lowest rate in the NFL 
 3. Los Angeles faces a quarterback slate that takes sacks less frequently than average 
 
 That's enough to hold back Garrett's projection, even coming off a record season in which he was the NFL's Defensive Player of the Year . And his age is a definite factor. While it's possible Garrett will be the same type of elite player well into his 30s, this model considers the drop-off of some previous edge rushers at this point in their careers.

 Do I think having Garrett fifth is underselling him a bit? I do, especially since the model is not considering the possibility of Aaron Donald unretiring and taking some heat off him. But there are real variables that are holding back Garrett's 2026 sack projection.

 

 

 

 6. Brian Burns , New York Giants 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.7 
 2025 sack total: 16.5

 Burns has always been a very good pass rusher -- and something of a pass rush win rate darling -- and exploded for 16.5 sacks in his second season in New York. And the Giants' pass rush has gotten even deeper.

 Those 16.5 sacks are enough to launch Burns, 28, into the top 10. But he has a few things working against him. His forecast is negatively affected by only having 8.5 sacks in 17 games in 2024. And while the Giants have a great pass rush, they aren't expected to be a great team. Middling teams don't play with a lead as often, which means fewer desperate opponents frequently passing to catch up.

 

 

 7. Nick Bosa , San Francisco 49ers 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.4 
 2025 sack total: 2

 This assumes that Bosa is healthy enough to play Week 1, which isn't a guarantee right now. The star edge rusher has been out for most of training camp with soreness and tendinitis as he works his way back from a torn ACL suffered last September.

 Despite the injury, Bosa's previous history is enough to include him in the top 10. In 2024, Bosa recorded nine sacks and also ranked fifth…

title: Why Drake Maye didn't play preseason; will it matter in Week 1?
summary: New England will kick off the season in Seattle for a Super Bowl rematch on Wednesday, Sept. 9.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Quick-hit thoughts and notes around the New England Patriots and NFL:

 1. Maye-less preseason: The preseason is over, and the final starting quarterback numbers are in.

 Of the league's 32 teams, 12 didn't play their established top quarterback in a game. That includes Drake Maye 's Patriots and Sam Darnold 's Seattle Seahawks , putting an added twist on the Super Bowl LX rematch that opens the 2026  regular season  on Wednesday, Sept. 9 ( NBC, 8:20 p.m. ET ).

 Will both quarterbacks be rusty without feeling game speed? Is the element of surprise in play more than it would have otherwise been?

 Those are among the compelling questions to be answered in Seattle.

 Also of note is that keeping Maye on the sideline throughout didn't appear to be Patriots coach Mike Vrabel's original intention.

 When Vrabel first connected with  Cleveland Browns  coach Todd Monken about plans for last Thursday's preseason finale, Monken shared they "had talked about initially wanting to play our starters -- get them a series or two." But Monken said both coaches ultimately came to the same conclusion: "We both felt like we were thin, especially up front on both sides of the ball. We just felt we'd be better off not playing our starters in the game."

 So it was a Maye-less, starter-less preseason in New England, which Vrabel explained further late Thursday night after his backups were thumped 37-13 in a low-energy, short-week loss.

 "We just wanted to try to get to the regular season with the guys that we had ... I know that's a difficult decision. I don't think there's a right or wrong answer," Vrabel said.

 

 How teams approach the preseason with their starting quarterback is a reflection, in part, of each coach and the organizational philosophy. Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott , for example, hasn't played in a preseason game since 2019. Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson hasn't played in a preseason game since 2021.

 Other teams that didn't have their starter play in the preseason this year include the Steelers ( Aaron Rodgers ), Colts ( Daniel Jones ), Jaguars ( Trevor Lawrence ), Chiefs ( Patrick Mahomes ), Eagles ( Jalen Hurts ), Lions ( Jared Goff ), Saints ( Tyler Shough ) and Rams ( Matthew Stafford ). In the case of the Colts' Jones and Chiefs' Mahomes, they are both returning from serious injuries sustained in 2025.

 Meanwhile, Lawrence landed in a similar situation as Maye in the sense that he had played last preseason under new coach Liam Coen but was held out this preseason. Coen said a driving factor in the decision was the work Lawrence received over four joint practices with the Saints, Panthers and Buccaneers. Last year, the Jaguars had just one joint practice.

 Some coaches believe those joint practices are equally as beneficial as preseason games, with teams more willing to run schemes they wouldn't in a game (when schemes would be on tape for the rest of the league to see). Another benefit is that practices are controlled, situations can be created that won't come up in a game, and quarterbacks can't be hit.

 The Patriots had three joint practices (one with the Colts, two with the Eagles), and Vrabel estimated that meant about 84 full-team reps for Maye.

 That was good work, but to some coaches, there's no substitute for a quarterback playing in a game when the defense can finish a sack or a hit in the pocket. Former Patriots coach Bill Belichick used to adopt that philosophy, saying at times, "You need 21 other guys out there so you can simulate football and the reactions of football."

 In a decision he seemed to be wrestling with at times, Vrabel was navigating that balance with Maye and the starters this preseason.

 2. Injuries mount: As the Patriots set their initial 53-man roster by Sunday's 6 p.m. ET deadline, they are dealing with a more significant injury report than they were at this time last year.

 They lost No. 2 tight end Julian Hill to a season-ending knee injury in the spring, and the surefire leader for the No. 3 running back role, Terrell Jennings , was placed on injured reserve and later reached an injury settlement. Top backup interior offensive lineman Ben Brown , top swing offensive tackle Marcus Bryant  and punter Bryce Baringer  are candidates to be placed on IR with a designation to return.

 

 That's one reason, along with shaky drafting before Vrabel's tenure began, that Vrabel referenced the Patriots as "not a very deep team" after the second preseason game.

 Executive vice president of player personnel Eliot Wolf noted the contrast.

 "We've had some injuries here that obviously thinned things out," he said. "We were pretty lucky, knock on wood, last year with some of the injury things that we had."

 3. Setting schedule : The Patriots' backups looked lethargic in Thursday's preseason finale, which wasn't entirely a surprise considering they were on the road after playing five days prior. A short week like this in the preseason from the NFL's schedule-makers seemed totally unnecessary.

 Vrabel gave players three straight days off to refill their tanks, saying it might benefit everyone to get away.

 They return Monday, with the next two practices set for Tuesday and Thursday. After a Friday off day, they then plan to practice Saturday, Sunday and Monday, Sept. 7, before departing for Seattle later on Monday.

 That will give them a full day in Seattle on Sept. 8 before the opener.

 4. They said it : "I have conversations with Christian, and I understand this is probably something that's difficult. ... Him and I communicate. Our players are always free to feel how they want to feel and you just have to stay patient and hope that we can continue to work to some sort of agreement." --  Vrabel, on cornerback Christian Gonzalez expressing frustration on contract negotiations 

 

 5. Jacas' learning curve : What does it look like when a rookie is away from the team all spring and doesn't practice until the first weekend of training camp after signing his contract late? Outside linebacker Gabe Jacas , the second-round pick from Illinois, is learning the answer to that question.

 Jacas played 81 snaps over three preseason games, was attacked with regularity on read-option plays, and sometimes looked to be out of position.

 Outside linebackers coach Mike Smith, who lauded Jacas for his work ethic and referred to him as "meaner than a wet mule," added context to the dynamic.

 "He didn't have the spring. We do a lot on defense and so a young player like that, you're just getting him lined up, know the defense and be in the right position," he said. "Then once he masters that, it's 'what are offenses doing to you? Where are the backfield sets? How is the tackle going to set you up?' There's so much more to it, and right now he's just getting lined up."

 Smith believes Jacas will be a "special player" in time.

 6. Ponder thought: Second-year outside linebacker Elijah Ponder , who spent training camp as a starter opposite Dre'Mont Jones with veteran Harold Landry III on the physically unable to perform list, has won over the confidence of the coaching staff.

 "Elijah has playmaking ability. He's versatile and can play multiple positions," defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr said on Boston sports radio WEEI. "I think the experience and success he had [in 2025] fed into his confidence. In joint practices, he looked like he belonged. He's going to be a big piece for the defense."

 

 7. Hall visit: With the Patriots' final preseason game on the road against the Browns, Vrabel had the team visit  the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio as part of the day-before-game itinerary. It provided an opportunity for Patriots legend and HOFer Andre Tippett to be the tour guide.

 "Having Tip be there to speak about the fraternity and his career -- he's a great Patriot. We were glad to be able to honor him in front of our football team," Vrabel said.
